questions.title: Governing Unity Catalog Across a Multi-Workspace, Multi-Business-Unit Metastore
questions.prompt: Your organization runs six Databricks workspaces -- one per business unit (Finance, Marketing, Supply Chain, HR, Engineering, and a shared Data Platform team) -- all attached to a single Unity Catalog metastore in the same region. Finance wants to lock down PII in their customer tables so only their own analysts can see raw SSNs, Supply Chain wants read access to Finance's cost-of-goods tables for a joint forecasting model, and the Data Platform team needs a consistent pattern for onboarding the next business unit without re-deriving governance rules from scratch. Design the catalog/schema structure, access-control model, and a scalable onboarding pattern for this environment.
questions.modelAnswer: A single metastore per region is correct here -- Unity Catalog is designed to be shared across many workspaces, and splitting it per business unit would duplicate governance work and break any cross-BU sharing. The structure should map one catalog per business unit (finance, supply_chain, hr, marketing, engineering) plus a shared catalog (e.g. shared_platform) for common reference/dimension data, with schemas inside each catalog separating raw/bronze from curated/gold layers. Access control is granted at the catalog or schema level using Unity Catalog's standard RBAC: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA grants scope who can even see an object exists, SELECT grants on specific tables or, for the SSN case, on a masked view rather than the raw table. For Finance's PII, the pattern is a dynamic view using CURRENT_USER()/IS_MEMBER() to mask the SSN column for everyone except a finance_pii_readers group, with the underlying raw table's SELECT grant restricted to a narrow service-principal/group -- row/column masking should live in SQL, not in downstream BI tool permissions, since that's the only enforcement point every consumer (notebooks, SQL warehouses, Power BI via Direct Lake) actually respects. For Supply Chain's cross-BU need, grant SELECT on finance.gold.cost_of_goods specifically to a supply_chain_analysts group rather than widening Finance's catalog-level grant, keeping the blast radius to one table. For onboarding, the Data Platform team should maintain this as Terraform/databricks provider code (catalog, schema, grant resources) rather than manual GRANT statements, so a new BU's catalog, standard schemas, and default group grants are created from a reviewed, repeatable module -- not tribal knowledge.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I get asked this, I start by pushing back gently on 'metastore per business unit' if anyone proposes it -- one metastore per region is the whole point of Unity Catalog, and splitting it defeats cross-BU sharing before you've even started. So I'd lay out catalog-per-BU plus one shared catalog for common dimensions, and get agreement on that shape first before touching a single GRANT statement. For the SSN problem specifically, I'd be direct that masking belongs in a SQL view, not in 'we'll just not give Marketing the Power BI workspace' -- because the moment someone connects a notebook directly to the raw table, that control is gone. For the Supply Chain ask, I'd resist the instinct to just grant them the whole Finance catalog because it's 'easier for now' -- one table, one grant, named group, done. And for onboarding, I'd tell the Data Platform team: if the sixth BU took a day of manual GRANTs, the tenth one will take two days and someone will typo a grant -- that's exactly the kind of thing that needs to be a Terraform module from day one, not a runbook.
commonMistakes: Proposes a separate metastore per business unit instead of one shared metastore with catalog-level separation
Masks PII in the BI tool or dashboard layer instead of a SQL-enforced dynamic view
Grants Supply Chain access to Finance's entire catalog instead of the single table they actually need
Treats onboarding as a manual GRANT runbook instead of codifying it as reusable IaC
Forgets USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA grants, so object-level SELECT grants silently fail to expose anything
keyPoints: Recommends one metastore per region, catalog-per-business-unit structure
Uses schema layering (raw/bronze vs curated/gold) within each catalog
Enforces PII masking via SQL dynamic views, not downstream tool permissions
Grants cross-BU access narrowly (table-level) rather than widening catalog grants
Codifies onboarding as IaC (Terraform databricks provider) rather than manual process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes correct catalog/metastore structure
Designs PII masking enforcement correctly
Scopes cross-BU access narrowly and justifies it
Proposes scalable, codified onboarding pattern

questions.title: Sharing Data With an External Partner Organization via Delta Sharing
questions.prompt: A retail client wants to share daily inventory-position data with three external logistics partners, none of whom run Databricks -- one uses Snowflake, one uses plain Python/pandas, and one wants a Power BI connection. The client is nervous about giving any partner more access than the single table they need, and legal wants an audit trail of who pulled what, when. Explain how you'd design this with Delta Sharing (open sharing vs Databricks-to-Databricks), what each partner actually needs on their end, and how you'd satisfy the audit requirement.
questions.modelAnswer: Because none of the three partners run Databricks, this has to be open (non-Databricks-to-Databricks) Delta Sharing rather than D2D sharing, which only works when the recipient also has a Unity Catalog metastore. Open sharing works by the provider creating a SHARE object containing only the specific table(s) to expose, then a RECIPIENT object scoped to that share; Databricks generates a bearer-token credential file (a recipient profile, typically delivered out of band) that the partner loads into whichever Delta Sharing client fits their stack -- Snowflake has a native Delta Sharing reader, the pandas partner uses the delta-sharing Python connector, and Power BI connects through the Delta Sharing Power BI connector. All three read the same underlying Delta table without a copy ever being made -- they query the shared table directly via the sharing protocol, which is the big win over 'export a CSV nightly.' To satisfy the access-scoping concern, I'd create one share per partner (or at minimum per-recipient table grants) containing only the inventory-position table, never the full schema or catalog, so even if a credential leaked, the blast radius is exactly one table. For the audit requirement, Unity Catalog's system tables (system.access.audit, plus Delta Sharing-specific recipient activity logs) record every recipient query against a shared table, including which recipient, which table version, and when -- I'd point legal to that rather than building a separate logging layer. I'd also set a credential expiration/rotation policy on each recipient token, since open sharing credentials are bearer tokens that don't expire by default unless configured to.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd open by ruling something out: because two of these three partners don't have their own Unity Catalog metastore, Databricks-to-Databricks sharing is off the table for all three -- we need open sharing, full stop, so everyone gets a consistent experience whether they're on Snowflake, pandas, or Power BI. From there I'd walk the client through exactly what a recipient does with their credential file -- it's just a token they load into a connector, not a database login -- and I'd push hard on one share per partner scoped to the single table, because 'it's easier to just share the schema' is how a logistics partner ends up seeing cost data they were never supposed to see. On the audit ask, I wouldn't propose building anything new -- I'd pull up the existing Unity Catalog access audit logs live and show legal that the who/what/when is already captured.
commonMistakes: Assumes Databricks-to-Databricks sharing works for partners without their own Unity Catalog metastore
Shares an entire schema/catalog instead of one scoped share per table
Doesn't realize open-sharing recipient credentials are bearer tokens without automatic expiration
Builds a custom export/ETL pipeline instead of using the Delta Sharing protocol directly
Can't point to a concrete audit mechanism when asked how access is logged
keyPoints: Correctly identifies open sharing as required (non-Databricks recipients)
Explains recipient profile/credential mechanism for non-Databricks clients
Scopes each share to the minimum table(s) needed per partner
Uses Unity Catalog system/audit tables to satisfy the legal audit requirement
Addresses credential expiration/rotation as an operational concern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes open vs Databricks-to-Databricks sharing
Explains partner-side consumption mechanics accurately
Scopes access narrowly per partner
Identifies a concrete audit mechanism

questions.title: Enforcing Data Quality Gates Across 40 Concurrent Lakeflow Pipelines
questions.prompt: Your platform team runs roughly 40 Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines feeding a shared gold layer that finance and executive dashboards depend on. Several incidents have occurred where a silently malformed upstream file let bad rows (negative revenue, null customer IDs) flow all the way to a dashboard before anyone noticed. Design a data-quality gating strategy using expectations that would have caught this, and explain the tradeoffs between expect, expect_or_drop, and expect_or_fail at this scale.
questions.modelAnswer: The three expectation modes differ only in what happens to a violating row, and choosing the right one per rule is the actual design problem here, not writing the SQL predicates. expect records and surfaces violations (visible in the pipeline event log/UI) but takes no corrective action -- appropriate for soft, informational signals a team wants to watch trend over time. expect_or_drop silently excludes violating rows from the output table while still counting and surfacing them in the event log -- appropriate for recoverable, row-level issues where losing a few bad rows doesn't change the meaning of the dataset. expect_or_fail stops the entire pipeline update on any violation -- appropriate for invariants that, if violated, actually corrupt downstream aggregates: a null customer_id breaking a join, or a negative revenue row skewing a sum, are exactly this category, and this incident happened because neither was enforced as a hard gate. The fix: map null customer_id and negative revenue to expect_or_fail at the bronze-to-silver boundary so a bad batch halts before reaching gold rather than silently reaching a dashboard; reserve expect_or_drop for genuinely recoverable issues (a missing but non-critical attribute). At 40-pipeline scale, the operational risk is duplicating these rule definitions independently in every pipeline file, so they should live in one shared Python module of expectation sets imported by every pipeline touching financial data, with violation rates reviewed via the pipeline event log on a recurring cadence rather than only when a dashboard incident forces someone to look.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by naming what actually went wrong: it wasn't that nobody validated the data, it's that the validation that existed lived in someone's downstream dashboard filter, which is the worst possible place for it, because by the time you're filtering in the dashboard, the bad row has already been written everywhere upstream of that filter too. So I'd walk through the severity ladder -- expect for 'watch it,' expect_or_drop for 'recoverable, quietly handle it,' expect_or_fail for 'this breaks the number, stop the pipeline' -- and map null customer IDs and negative revenue straight to expect_or_fail, because those are the two things from the actual incident. Then I'd make the case that with 40 pipelines, we can't have 40 copies of this logic drifting independently, so this becomes a shared module the moment it's written, not a follow-up task.
commonMistakes: Uses expect_or_drop for every rule regardless of severity, silently losing rows that should have hard-failed the pipeline
Uses expect_or_fail for soft/informational rules, causing unnecessary pipeline outages
Duplicates expectation definitions across 40 pipelines instead of sharing them from a common module
Never reviews the pipeline event log for violation rates, so a slowly rising drop rate goes unnoticed
Treats expectations as a one-time setup rather than something revisited as upstream sources change
keyPoints: Distinguishes expect (warn), expect_or_drop (quarantine), expect_or_fail (hard stop) and when each applies
Maps critical invariants (null customer_id, negative revenue) to expect_or_fail at the bronze/silver boundary
Uses expect_or_drop for recoverable row-level issues with dropped-row visibility
Shares expectation definitions across pipelines instead of duplicating per-pipeline
Monitors violation rates via the pipeline event log, not just pass/fail

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the three expectation modes and when to use each
Maps the actual incident to a concrete fix
Addresses sharing/consistency of rules across 40 pipelines
Proposes ongoing monitoring of violation rates

questions.title: Choosing Triggered vs. Continuous Mode Across a Pipeline Fleet, and Catching Failures Early
questions.prompt: Your team operates a mix of around 40 Lakeflow pipelines: some feed hourly executive dashboards, a few feed a near-real-time fraud-alerting table, and most are overnight batch loads. Right now everything runs in triggered mode on a cron schedule, and last week a fraud-alerting pipeline's upstream source went stale for three hours before anyone noticed because its scheduled run 'succeeded' on zero new rows. Decide which pipelines should move to continuous mode, and design a monitoring approach across the fleet that would catch a 'succeeded but suspiciously empty' failure like this one.
questions.modelAnswer: Triggered mode runs the pipeline once to process whatever's new, then shuts compute down -- cost scales with data volume and run frequency, which is exactly right for hourly dashboards and overnight batch loads where a few minutes of added latency is irrelevant. Continuous mode keeps the pipeline and its compute running permanently, processing data as it lands with minimal latency, but it bills for that compute 24/7 regardless of whether data is flowing -- it should be reserved for the handful of cases where staleness itself has a real cost, which here is specifically the fraud-alerting pipeline, not the dashboards or batch loads. Moving everything to continuous would be a cost mistake, not a resilience improvement. But the actual incident wasn't caused by the pipeline mode at all -- a scheduled run that processes zero new rows still reports 'succeeded,' because success and freshness are different signals, and that gap exists whether the pipeline is triggered or continuous. The real fix is monitoring: use the pipeline event log to track rows processed per run per table, and alert separately when a stream that should always have traffic goes beyond a defined staleness window (e.g., no new rows in 15 minutes for the fraud table) with no new data, distinct from ordinary pipeline failure alerting. That staleness threshold should be set per pipeline based on its actual expected cadence, not a single fleet-wide number, since 15 minutes is alarming for a real-time fraud feed and meaningless for an overnight batch load.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team the real bug here isn't the pipeline mode, it's that we were treating 'succeeded' and 'healthy' as the same thing -- a run that processes zero rows when it should have processed thousands is not a success, even though Lakeflow will happily report it as one. So before I talk about continuous mode at all, I'd get freshness-based alerting in place using the pipeline event log, scoped per pipeline since a 15-minute staleness threshold means something very different for the fraud table than for an overnight batch job. Then, separately, I'd move only the fraud-alerting pipeline to continuous mode, and I'd be upfront with finance that this is a real cost tradeoff -- it runs 24/7 whether or not fraud events are actually happening -- which is exactly why I wouldn't extend it to the dashboards or batch jobs where triggered mode is already the right answer.
commonMistakes: Moves most/all pipelines to continuous mode instead of reserving it for genuinely latency-sensitive cases
Doesn't account for continuous mode's always-on compute cost vs triggered mode's pay-only-when-running cost
Equates pipeline success status with data freshness/health, missing the zero-rows-processed case
Builds per-pipeline ad hoc alerting instead of a consistent freshness-SLA check across the fleet
Sets a single staleness threshold for every pipeline regardless of its actual expected cadence
keyPoints: Correctly scopes continuous mode to the fraud-alerting pipeline only, keeping batch/dashboard pipelines triggered
Explains the cost/latency tradeoff between triggered and continuous mode
Identifies that pipeline success status alone doesn't indicate data freshness/health
Designs row-count/freshness-based alerting using the pipeline event log
Proposes fleet-wide monitoring with per-pipeline SLA thresholds, not a single global threshold

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly decides which pipelines should move to continuous mode and why
Explains the cost/latency tradeoff accurately
Diagnoses the real gap (success does not equal freshness) in the incident
Designs a concrete fleet-wide monitoring/alerting approach

questions.title: Cutting a $40K/Month Databricks Compute Bill Without Hurting SLAs
questions.prompt: Finance flags that Databricks compute spend has grown to roughly $40,000/month, and asks you, as the platform lead, to cut it meaningfully within a quarter without missing any existing SLA. A quick audit shows: most nightly ETL jobs run on long-lived all-purpose clusters that stay up all day 'just in case,' autoscaling is disabled almost everywhere, and a few ad hoc analyst notebooks are attached to the same large cluster as production jobs. Walk through where you'd cut first, what you would NOT touch, and how you'd verify savings didn't come at the cost of reliability.
questions.modelAnswer: The highest-impact, lowest-risk cut is moving scheduled ETL jobs off all-purpose clusters onto job clusters: an all-purpose cluster that stays up all day bills continuously regardless of utilization, while a job cluster spins up for the run and terminates on completion, so cost becomes proportional to actual compute time rather than wall-clock uptime -- this is almost always the single biggest lever in an audit like this one. Second, enable autoscaling with min/max bounds informed by historical load (not arbitrary defaults), so clusters stop paying for idle headroom sized for a worst-case that rarely occurs. Third, separate the ad hoc analyst notebooks onto their own interactive cluster with an auto-termination policy (e.g., terminate after 30-60 minutes idle), since sharing a cluster with production jobs means a runaway exploratory query can inflate the sizing production actually needs, or contend with it directly. Spot/preemptible instances are worth evaluating for fault-tolerant batch workloads where a preempted worker just gets replaced and retried, but I would explicitly exclude anything SLA-critical or stateful -- the fraud-alerting continuous pipeline's cluster, for example, should stay on-demand, because preemption risk there is a business risk, not a reliability inconvenience, and correctness/latency guarantees are not the place to shave compute cost. To verify savings are real and not masking a reliability regression, I'd tag every cluster by team/job for cost attribution, compare before/after DBU and cloud spend per workload, and specifically watch SLA-miss rate and job duration for two to three weeks post-change, since a change that looks fine under one week's load might not hold under a spike.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk finance through this as 'there's one obvious lever and three smaller ones, plus a line I won't cross.' The obvious lever: these ETL jobs don't need an all-purpose cluster sitting up all day, they need a job cluster that exists for the run and disappears -- that alone is usually most of the savings in a situation like this. The smaller levers are autoscaling with real bounds instead of none, and getting the analysts off the production cluster so their queries stop driving its sizing. The line I won't cross is the fraud-alerting pipeline's cluster -- I'd tell finance directly that's not a cost-cutting candidate, because a preempted spot instance there isn't an inconvenience, it's a missed fraud alert. And I wouldn't declare victory off one good week -- I'd watch SLA-miss rate for a few weeks before telling anyone the savings are safe.
commonMistakes: Suggests shrinking or spot-pricing a cluster backing an SLA-critical or stateful streaming workload
Treats autoscaling as a free win without setting sensible min/max bounds, causing scale-up thrashing
Doesn't separate ad hoc analyst workloads from production job clusters
Declares savings based on one day of lower cost without watching for SLA regressions over several weeks
Misses that all-purpose-vs-job-cluster billing is usually the single biggest lever available
keyPoints: Identifies all-purpose-vs-job-cluster mismatch as the primary cost driver
Enables autoscaling with bounds informed by historical load, not arbitrary defaults
Isolates ad hoc/analyst workloads from production clusters
Uses spot/preemptible instances selectively, excluding SLA-critical or stateful workloads
Verifies savings against SLA-miss rate over a meaningful window, not a single day

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies the highest-impact cost lever (job vs all-purpose clusters)
Correctly scopes where autoscaling/spot should and should not be used
Addresses workload isolation (ad hoc vs production)
Proposes a sound verification method against SLA risk

questions.title: Diagnosing a Job That Shuffles 40 Million Rows Into Eight Wildly Uneven Partitions
questions.prompt: A nightly Spark job joins a 40-million-row transactions table to a dimension table on customer_id, then aggregates. The Spark UI shows the job spends most of its wall-clock time on a single task out of 200, while the other 199 finish in seconds -- and that one task's input partition is roughly 100x larger than the rest. Explain what's actually happening at the shuffle level, why it's specific to this join, and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: This is data skew in the join key, not a resource problem. Spark's shuffle for a join hash-partitions both sides by the join key, sending every row with the same customer_id to the same partition/task -- that's the whole mechanism, and it means if one or a few customer_id values (say, a shared 'unknown' or bulk-account ID) account for a disproportionate share of the 40 million rows, every one of those rows lands in the same single task regardless of how many total partitions you've configured, while the other 199 tasks handle the genuinely distinct, evenly-spread keys and finish quickly. More executors or memory won't fix this, because the problem isn't total capacity, it's that one task has 100x the work of the others and nothing can parallelize work that's all been assigned to a single task. The first thing to check is Adaptive Query Execution's skew join handling (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled), which detects oversized shuffle partitions at runtime and automatically splits them -- this requires no code change and should be tried before anything manual. If AQE doesn't catch this specific pattern, the manual fix is salting: add a random sub-key to the skewed value(s) on the fact side, explode the dimension side so a matching row exists for every possible salt bucket of that key, and join on the composite key -- this spreads the hot key's rows across many tasks instead of one, while leaving the non-skewed 99%+ of the data untouched. Diagnosing this correctly means actually looking at the Spark UI's per-task shuffle read size before proposing a fix, not guessing from wall-clock time alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd say is: don't add executors yet. A single straggling task out of 200 while everything else finishes in seconds is the signature of data skew, not insufficient capacity, and throwing more compute at it won't touch the one task that's doing 100x the work. I'd go to the Spark UI stage detail and confirm the shuffle read size on that task before I say another word, because I want evidence, not a guess. Then I'd try AQE's skew join setting first, since it's a zero-code-change flag that handles a lot of these cases automatically now. If that doesn't resolve it, I'd explain salting to the team as 'we're giving the one overloaded key a bunch of fake sub-identities so Spark spreads its rows across many tasks instead of jamming them all into one' -- and I'd be clear we only need to do that for the specific hot key, not the whole dataset.
commonMistakes: Assumes the slow task is a resource/executor problem and just adds more executors
Doesn't check the Spark UI's task-level shuffle read size to confirm it's actually skew
Jumps straight to manual salting without first trying AQE's built-in skew join handling
Salts every key uniformly instead of targeting just the known skewed value(s)
Confuses this with a broadcast-join sizing problem when the dimension table isn't actually the issue
keyPoints: Correctly identifies data skew in the join key as the root cause
Explains hash-partitioning mechanics of the shuffle and why skew creates one oversized partition
Diagnoses using Spark UI task/shuffle metrics before proposing a fix
Proposes AQE skew join handling and/or manual salting appropriately
Considers isolating and broadcast-joining a small known hot key set

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses data skew as the cause, not a resource problem
Explains shuffle/hash-partitioning mechanics accurately
Proposes AQE skew handling and/or salting correctly
Demonstrates proper diagnostic approach using Spark UI metrics

questions.title: Sizing and Governing Fabric Capacity Across 15 Business-Unit Workspaces
questions.prompt: Your organization is consolidating 15 separate Power BI Pro workspaces onto Microsoft Fabric capacity, shared across business units with wildly different usage patterns -- Finance runs heavy month-end batch refreshes, Marketing runs occasional ad hoc exploration, and one data science team runs Spark notebooks against the same capacity. Within the first month on a single F64 capacity, Finance's month-end refresh throttles everyone else's reports for several hours. Diagnose what's happening with capacity smoothing/throttling, and propose both a short-term and long-term fix, including whether chargeback should factor in.
questions.modelAnswer: A Fabric capacity consumes one shared pool of Capacity Units (CUs) across every Fabric workload on that SKU -- Power BI refresh, Spark notebooks, pipelines, warehouse queries -- and Fabric uses a smoothing algorithm that spreads background operations' CU consumption over a rolling window (roughly 24 hours) rather than charging it instantly, specifically to absorb normal bursts without throttling. What's happening here is that Finance's sustained month-end batch demand exceeds the capacity's throughput even after smoothing, so Fabric throttles: first delaying background/scheduled operations, and if demand still exceeds capacity, degrading or rejecting interactive operations -- which is exactly what the other business units are feeling as 'throttled reports.' This is designed behavior under genuine overload, not a bug. Short-term fix: reschedule Finance's heaviest refresh window to off-peak hours when other BUs aren't interactively using the capacity, and/or temporarily scale the SKU up (F64 to F128) during month-end, scaling back down afterward -- Fabric capacities can be resized without any data movement since it's purely a compute-tier change. Long-term, the real issue is architectural: co-mingling a monthly batch spike with 14 other units' daily interactive SLA on one capacity is a workload mismatch, not just a sizing problem, so I'd evaluate splitting Finance's batch-heavy workload onto its own dedicated capacity from the interactive BI workloads. Chargeback should absolutely factor in -- Fabric's capacity metrics app reports CU consumption per workspace, which gives a concrete way to make Finance's month-end cost visible to Finance rather than it being invisibly subsidized by, or blamed on, the other 14 units.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by telling the team this isn't Fabric misbehaving -- smoothing and throttling are designed behavior, and what we're seeing is sustained demand genuinely exceeding what one capacity can absorb, even with smoothing doing its job. Short term, I'd look at two cheap levers before anything expensive: can Finance's refresh move to a quieter window, and can we burst the SKU up just for month-end and back down after, since that's a pure compute-tier change with zero data movement. But I'd be honest with leadership that the real fix is architectural -- putting a monthly batch spike on the same capacity as 14 teams' daily interactive reporting was always going to collide eventually, so I'd push for giving Finance its own capacity. And I wouldn't leave chargeback as an afterthought -- the capacity metrics app already tells us exactly how many CUs each workspace burns, so I'd use that to make Finance's own cost visible to Finance, not something the other 14 teams quietly absorb.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a bug to report to Microsoft rather than understanding smoothing/throttling as designed behavior
Just scales the SKU up permanently instead of considering workload separation or scheduling fixes
Doesn't distinguish background/scheduled throttling from interactive-operation throttling
Ignores the capacity metrics app as the tool to actually attribute CU usage per workspace
Proposes chargeback without a concrete attribution mechanism
keyPoints: Explains Fabric's CU smoothing and throttling mechanism accurately
Diagnoses sustained batch demand exceeding capacity even after smoothing as the root cause
Proposes a viable short-term fix (reschedule and/or temporary scale-up)
Proposes workload separation (dedicated capacity) as the long-term architectural fix
Ties chargeback to concrete per-workspace CU attribution via the capacity metrics app

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains smoothing/throttling mechanics
Diagnoses the actual root cause (sustained demand exceeding capacity)
Proposes sound short-term and long-term fixes
Addresses chargeback with a concrete attribution mechanism

questions.title: Direct Lake Fell Back to DirectQuery for a 200-Million-Row Semantic Model
questions.prompt: A finance semantic model built on Direct Lake was performing well, but after a recent schema change and a large backfill, users report dashboards have become noticeably slower, and the Fabric monitoring hub shows the model is now falling back to DirectQuery on most queries. At enterprise scale with 200+ million rows, explain why Direct Lake falls back, how you'd confirm that's actually happening, and what you'd change to get Direct Lake performance back.
questions.modelAnswer: Direct Lake reads Delta Parquet files directly into Fabric's in-memory analytics engine without a separate import/refresh step, which is why it's normally fast -- but the underlying Delta table has to meet certain conditions to stay eligible for Direct Lake; when it doesn't, Fabric transparently falls back to DirectQuery (querying the lakehouse via the SQL engine instead), so the report still returns correct results, just much slower, often with no obvious error surfaced to the end user. Common fallback triggers after a schema change plus a large backfill: a burst of many small Parquet files or excessive uncompacted table history from the backfill without an OPTIMIZE/VACUUM pass, use of a Delta feature or version state Direct Lake doesn't support, or the Parquet files not having V-Order applied (Fabric's engine is specifically tuned for V-Order Parquet). The guardrails on row/column count for the capacity's SKU are also worth checking, since a model that's grown past them during the backfill would fall back for that reason alone. To confirm this is actually what's happening rather than guessing from user-perceived latency, I'd check the Fabric Monitoring Hub's semantic model query diagnostics, which explicitly report Direct Lake vs. DirectQuery fallback events per query. The fix: run OPTIMIZE (with V-Order) on the affected Delta tables after the backfill, review table history/file count against the Direct Lake guardrails for the capacity's SKU, and if row/column count has genuinely outgrown the SKU's limits, either prune the model to needed columns or move to a larger capacity tier -- all before considering a switch to Import mode.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd tell the team is that this isn't broken -- Direct Lake falling back to DirectQuery is a silent, correctness-preserving behavior, not an error, which is exactly why nobody got an alert and users just experienced it as 'slow.' I wouldn't guess at the cause from latency alone -- I'd go straight to the Monitoring Hub's query diagnostics, which will tell us plainly whether we're actually falling back and on which queries. Given the timing lines up with a schema change and a big backfill, my first suspicion is a pile of small, uncompacted files from that backfill, so I'd run OPTIMIZE with V-Order on those tables before I touch anything else. And I'd check the model's row and column count against this capacity's Direct Lake guardrails too, since a backfill is exactly the kind of event that can push a model past a limit nobody was watching.
commonMistakes: Assumes DirectQuery fallback means something is broken rather than an intentional, silent correctness-preserving behavior
Doesn't check Monitoring Hub fallback diagnostics, guessing at the cause from latency alone
Forgets to run OPTIMIZE/V-Order after a large backfill, leaving many small files behind
Doesn't check the semantic model against the capacity SKU's Direct Lake row/column guardrails
Recommends switching to Import mode as the only fix instead of first addressing table maintenance
keyPoints: Explains Direct Lake's in-memory read mechanism and why it falls back to DirectQuery
Identifies likely fallback triggers tied to the recent schema change and backfill (small files, missing OPTIMIZE/V-Order)
Uses Monitoring Hub diagnostics to confirm fallback rather than guessing

questions.title: Standardizing Git-Based CI/CD Across 15 Fabric Workspaces
questions.prompt: As the platform lead, you're introducing Git integration and deployment pipelines to 15 Fabric workspaces that have so far been edited directly in the service with no version control. Two concerns from the team: (1) business analysts want to keep editing reports directly in the Fabric UI without learning Git, and (2) the data engineering team wants a real dev to test to prod promotion flow with no manual re-wiring of connections between environments. Design the approach.
questions.modelAnswer: Fabric's Git integration syncs a workspace's items to a branch in Azure DevOps/GitHub; changes made directly in the Fabric UI commit to that branch automatically or on manual sync, so analysts genuinely keep editing in the familiar canvas while still getting version history, diffability for most item types, and rollback underneath them without ever touching a Git client -- this addresses concern (1) directly, since the value of version control doesn't require the editor to use Git. For the dev-to-test-to-prod flow, Git integration and Deployment Pipelines are two separate features that need to be paired: Git integration captures changes with branch-based isolation per environment workspace, while Deployment Pipelines promotes content across a defined sequence of workspaces (dev, test, prod). The piece that solves concern (2) specifically is deployment rules configured per stage within the pipeline -- these let you map a dev workspace's lakehouse/warehouse connection, parameter, or connection string to the corresponding test/prod equivalent automatically on every promotion, so engineers never hand-edit a connection string after a promotion. Recommended structure: each business unit's workspace gets its own Git-connected dev workspace, feeding into a shared or per-BU deployment pipeline through test and prod stages; engineering-heavy items (notebooks, pipelines) can use branch-per-feature with PR review if the team wants it, while analysts stay on a simpler main-branch auto-sync pattern for reports, since their workflow doesn't need PR gates to get the version-control benefit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd open with the thing that usually surprises people: analysts don't need to learn Git for any of this to work. Git integration runs underneath the normal Fabric UI -- they keep editing reports exactly as they do today, and the commits just happen in the background. That solves concern one without a single training session. For concern two, I'd be careful to separate two features people often conflate: Git integration gives you version control, Deployment Pipelines gives you promotion across environments, and you need both working together here. The piece I'd spend the most time on is deployment rules, because that's specifically what stops someone from having to manually re-point a connection string every time something gets promoted to test or prod -- without that, this whole effort just trades 'manual editing' for 'manual re-wiring,' which isn't actually progress.
commonMistakes: Assumes Git integration requires analysts to learn Git commands, missing that it works underneath normal UI editing
Conflates Git integration with Deployment Pipelines, treating them as the same feature
Doesn't configure deployment rules, leaving connection strings to be manually re-wired after every promotion
Puts every workspace on a single shared branch with no environment isolation
Underestimates that not every Fabric item type diffs/merges cleanly in Git, and doesn't flag that limitation
keyPoints: Explains that Git integration works underneath the Fabric UI without requiring analysts to use Git directly
Distinguishes Git integration (version control) from Deployment Pipelines (environment promotion)
Uses deployment rules to auto-remap connections per stage, eliminating manual re-wiring
Designs a workspace-per-environment structure feeding a shared deployment pipeline

Correctly distinguishes Git integration from Deployment Pipelines
