questions.title: Designing Active/Active vs. Active/Passive Kafka Replication Across Two Data Centers
questions.prompt: Your org runs Kafka clusters in two data centers (East and West) for disaster-recovery purposes. The East cluster currently serves all production traffic; West is idle, synced via a MirrorMaker-style replication tool. Leadership wants to know if moving to an active/active setup -- both regions serving writes -- would improve resilience, and what it would actually cost in complexity. Compare active/passive and active/active replication topologies for this scenario and make a recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer: Active/passive -- one cluster authoritative for writes, the other kept in sync via cross-cluster mirroring and promoted to primary only on failover -- is operationally simple: there's a single source of truth, no possibility of write conflicts, and a bounded (if nontrivial) failover story. Its real cost is idle standby capacity and the discipline required to keep offset translation actually tested, not just configured. Active/active, where both clusters accept writes for at least some topics, eliminates the idle-capacity waste and can lower write latency for geographically distributed producers, but introduces genuine complexity: Kafka itself provides no cross-cluster transaction or global ordering guarantee, so topics written in both data centers need either disjoint partitioning (producers in each DC write to DC-specific partitions or topics, avoiding true conflict) or an explicit conflict-resolution strategy at the application layer -- in practice, 'active/active' usually means two independently-written topic sets merged downstream, not one topic accepting genuinely concurrent conflicting writes from both sides. Given that the stated goal here is disaster recovery, not geo-distributed write latency or idle-capacity utilization, I'd recommend staying active/passive and hardening it rather than adding active/active's complexity for a problem it doesn't solve: specifically, verify that the mirroring tool's consumer-offset translation is tested in an actual failover drill, not just configured (replicated offsets don't automatically mean a consumer resumes at the right position), and establish a documented RPO and RTO measured during that drill rather than assumed from the fact that replication is 'running.' Moving to active/active would add significant engineering cost without addressing the DR goal, unless there's a separate latency or capacity driver that hasn't been stated.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I compare anything, I'd ask leadership what problem active/active is actually supposed to solve, because if the answer is still 'disaster recovery,' active/active doesn't get us anything active/passive doesn't already provide -- it just adds complexity we don't need. I'd walk through why: active/active sounds like more resilience, but Kafka doesn't give you cross-cluster write ordering or conflict resolution for free, so in practice you end up with two separately-written streams that need merging downstream, which is real engineering work, not a configuration flag. What I'd actually push for is hardening what we have -- specifically, running a real failover drill to see whether our consumer offset translation actually works, because 'replication is configured' and 'failover works' are two different claims, and right now we've only verified the first one.
commonMistakes: Recommends active/active without identifying any actual latency/capacity driver, just for 'resilience'
Assumes mirrored consumer offsets are automatically correct on failover without testing
Treats active/active as 'both clusters accept all writes freely' without addressing conflict/ordering
Doesn't define or measure RPO/RTO before declaring either topology adequate
Ignores the real engineering cost of active/active for a goal (DR) that active/passive already serves
keyPoints: Explains active/passive and active/active topologies accurately, including offset translation challenges
Correctly identifies that true active/active requires conflict resolution or partition-level write isolation
Matches the recommendation to the actual stated goal (DR) rather than defaulting to the trendier option
Proposes a concrete RPO/RTO measurement via failover drill as the real improvement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains both replication topologies and their tradeoffs
Correctly identifies the complexity cost of active/active (conflict/ordering)
Makes a recommendation matched to the actual stated goal
Proposes concrete RPO/RTO validation via failover testing

questions.title: Preventing a Breaking Schema Change From Taking Down Six Downstream Consumers
questions.prompt: Twelve teams produce and consume events through a shared Confluent Schema Registry. Last month, a producer team renamed a field in their Avro schema without realizing six other teams' consumers depended on it, breaking all of them simultaneously in production. As the platform team, design a schema governance model -- compatibility modes, review process, and tooling -- that prevents this from recurring without making every team file a ticket for every change.
questions.modelAnswer: Set the registry's compatibility mode to BACKWARD at the subject level (or BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for subjects with many historical consumer versions still in flight), so the registry itself rejects a schema registration that isn't compatible with the prior version -- a straight field rename is exactly the kind of change BACKWARD compatibility catches and blocks, because to a consumer, an old field disappearing and a new one appearing looks identical to a deletion plus an addition, which breaks any consumer still reading the old field name. This moves the check from 'someone remembers to look' to 'the registry enforces it automatically at registration time,' which is the actual fix -- no amount of process compensates for an enforcement gap like the one that caused this incident. For the producer team's underlying need (they wanted a clearer field name), the safe evolution pattern is additive: add the new field alongside the old one, mark the old one deprecated, migrate consumers over an announced window, and only remove the old field after confirmed migration -- never a rename as a single atomic operation. To avoid a ticket-per-change burden, enforcement should live in CI, not human review: a producer's CI pipeline calls the registry's compatibility-check endpoint against the candidate schema before merge, so compatible, additive changes sail through with zero human gatekeeping, and only an actually-incompatible change fails the build with a clear message -- which is also the right moment for a human conversation to happen. A lightweight ownership model, where each subject is owned by a team and consumers register their dependency on a subject, lets a producer query who's actually affected before proposing a change, rather than discovering it in production.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real lesson from this incident isn't 'be more careful' -- it's that we were relying on a human remembering something the registry could have enforced automatically. So the first thing I'd do is set BACKWARD compatibility on the subject and show the team that this exact rename would now be rejected at registration time, full stop, no process required. Then I'd address what the producer team actually wanted, which is a clearer field name -- I'd walk them through add-new-field, deprecate-old-field, migrate, remove, instead of a rename, because that gets them the outcome without the breaking change. And I'd be clear that none of this should mean more tickets -- it should mean the compatibility check runs in their CI pipeline automatically, so the only time a human needs to get involved is when something is genuinely incompatible, which is exactly when you'd want a conversation anyway.
commonMistakes: Proposes a manual change-review process instead of registry-enforced compatibility checking
Doesn't recognize a field rename as equivalent to delete+add from a consumer's perspective
Sets compatibility mode too loosely (NONE or FORWARD) when BACKWARD is what actually protects existing consumers
Requires a ticket/approval for every schema change instead of gating via automated CI compatibility checks
Has no mechanism for producers to know who consumes a given subject before making a change
keyPoints: Sets BACKWARD (or BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE) compatibility mode to make the registry reject breaking changes automatically
Correctly identifies a field rename as a breaking change under backward compatibility
Proposes additive-then-deprecate-then-remove as the safe evolution pattern instead of atomic renames
Gates schema changes via CI compatibility checks rather than manual ticket-based review
Maintains consumer/subject ownership visibility so impact can be assessed before a change ships

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes and justifies a compatibility mode that would have caught this incident
Correctly identifies why a rename is a breaking change
Proposes a safe schema evolution pattern
Designs a low-friction, CI-enforced governance process

questions.title: Lambda vs. Kappa for a Hybrid Databricks + Fabric + Kafka Analytics Platform
questions.prompt: Your org ingests clickstream events via Kafka, lands them through both a real-time path (Fabric Eventstreams/Eventhouse for live dashboards) and a batch path (Databricks Lakeflow pipelines landing to Delta for historical analytics and ML features), and has started seeing the two paths disagree on daily totals by a few percent -- a classic symptom of running two independently-built pipelines over the same source. Compare the lambda and kappa architecture patterns for this specific stack, and recommend which one actually fits, given you have both Databricks and Fabric in play, not a single processing engine.
questions.modelAnswer: Lambda architecture runs two independent pipelines over the same source -- a fast/streaming path for low-latency approximate results and a slow/batch path for the authoritative, corrected historical view -- which is actually what this org already has: Eventstreams/Eventhouse as the fast path, Lakeflow batch-to-Delta as the slow path. The daily-totals mismatch isn't a sign lambda is broken; it's the expected consequence of maintaining two separately-coded transformation logics over the same events, which drift apart in small ways (different windowing, different late-event handling, different dedup logic) unless deliberately kept in sync -- that dual-codebase drift is lambda's core, well-known maintenance cost, not a bug unique to this org. Kappa architecture replaces this with a single stream-processing pipeline that is also used, via reprocessing from retained Kafka history, to produce the 'batch' historical view -- there's only one code path, so by construction the fast and slow results can't disagree, at the cost of needing a processing engine capable of both the real-time and large-scale reprocessing workloads, plus Kafka retention long enough to support full reprocessing. Given that this org runs Fabric Eventstreams (a managed, Fabric-specific real-time engine) and Databricks Lakeflow (a genuinely separate batch engine), a pure kappa architecture isn't straightforwardly available -- there's no single engine here that does both. The pragmatic recommendation: keep the lambda-like shape, since replacing either platform isn't on the table, but fix the actual drift source directly by expressing the two paths' windowing/dedup/late-event logic as closely as the two engines allow from one shared specification, and add continuous automated reconciliation between Eventhouse's running total and Delta's batch total, alerting on drift beyond a defined tolerance, rather than discovering the mismatch by someone noticing dashboards disagree.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on 'should we move to kappa' as the framing, because kappa assumes one engine that can do both real-time processing and full historical reprocessing, and we don't have that -- we have Fabric Eventstreams doing one job and Databricks Lakeflow doing a genuinely different one. So this is structurally a lambda architecture whether we name it that or not, and the mismatch we're seeing is exactly the cost lambda is known for: two independently maintained pipelines over the same source will drift unless we actively keep them in sync. I wouldn't propose ripping out either platform to chase a pure kappa design -- that's a much bigger and more expensive conversation than this incident calls for. What I'd actually propose is getting the two paths' windowing and late-event logic as close to identical as the two engines allow, and then putting a daily reconciliation check between Eventhouse's total and Delta's total so the next drift gets caught by an alert, not by someone noticing a dashboard looks off.
commonMistakes: Recommends kappa without acknowledging it requires a single processing engine capable of both real-time and reprocessing, which this stack doesn't have
Treats the daily-totals mismatch as a bug in one pipeline rather than the structural consequence of lambda's dual-codebase design
Proposes a full platform consolidation as the only fix, ignoring cost/migration reality
Doesn't propose any ongoing reconciliation/drift-detection mechanism, leaving the same problem to recur silently
Confuses lambda/kappa with simply 'batch vs streaming' without the shared-source, dual-path definition
keyPoints: Correctly defines lambda (dual independent pipelines) and kappa (single reprocessable stream pipeline) architectures
Identifies the daily-totals drift as the expected cost of lambda's dual-codebase design, not a one-off bug
Recognizes kappa isn't cleanly available given two separate engines (Fabric Eventstreams, Databricks Lakeflow)
Recommends a pragmatic fix: shared transformation logic plus continuous reconciliation, not a platform rewrite

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains lambda and kappa architectures
Correctly diagnoses the drift as inherent to the current lambda-like design
Correctly reasons about engine constraints (no single engine spans both paths here)
Proposes a pragmatic, implementable recommendation

questions.title: Fix a Skewed 40-Million-Row Join With Key Salting
questions.prompt: The join from the earlier skew diagnosis (40M-row transactions table joining a dimension table on customer_id, with one customer_id responsible for roughly 60% of all rows) needs an actual code fix, not just a diagnosis. Write the PySpark code to salt the skewed key and produce a correct, balanced join.
questions.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

SALT_BUCKETS = 20
skewed_keys = ["CUST_00000"]  # known hot key(s) from prior diagnosis

# Split the fact table: skewed rows get a random salt, normal rows get salt = 0
txns_salted = transactions.withColumn(
    "salt",
    F.when(F.col("customer_id").isin(skewed_keys), (F.rand() * SALT_BUCKETS).cast("int"))
     .otherwise(F.lit(0))
)

# Explode the dimension table: one row per salt bucket for the skewed keys, one row (salt=0) for everyone else
dim_exploded = dim_customer.withColumn(
    "salt",
    F.explode(
        F.when(F.col("customer_id").isin(skewed_keys), F.array([F.lit(i) for i in range(SALT_BUCKETS)]))
         .otherwise(F.array(F.lit(0)))
    )
)

joined = txns_salted.join(
    dim_exploded,
    on=["customer_id", "salt"],
    how="inner"
).drop("salt")
questions.modelAnswer: Salting breaks up the one oversized shuffle partition created by hash-partitioning on a skewed key, by artificially sub-dividing that key into SALT_BUCKETS synthetic sub-keys so the shuffle spreads its rows across many partitions instead of one. The fact table gets a random salt column, but only for rows carrying a known skewed key -- everyone else gets salt=0 and is otherwise untouched. The dimension table must be exploded so it has a matching row for every salt bucket the skewed key could have produced; without this, the join on (customer_id, salt) would only match salt=0 dimension rows and silently drop the skewed-key fact rows entirely, turning a performance fix into a correctness bug. The result is the same logical join -- the skewed key's rows are now parallelized across SALT_BUCKETS tasks, and the non-skewed 99%+ of the data produces an identical result to the unsalted join since both sides use salt=0. The cost is a small duplication of dimension rows for the skewed key only, negligible if the dimension table is small. This is the manual version of what AQE's skew join optimization now does automatically in most cases -- worth trying spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled first, reaching for manual salting only when AQE doesn't detect or handle this specific pattern.
questions.professionalAnswer: The part people usually get wrong the first time they try this is forgetting to explode the dimension side. If you only salt the fact table and join on (customer_id, salt) against an unmodified dimension table, every row you just salted to anything other than 0 silently fails to match and disappears from the output -- you've fixed the skew and broken the join at the same time, and it's easy not to notice because the job runs fast now, which looks like success. So I always build this in two matched halves: salt the hot key on the fact side, then make sure the dimension side has one row per possible salt value for that same key before I even run it. I'd also check AQE's skew join setting first, since a lot of what used to require this by hand is now handled automatically, and I'd rather not maintain custom salting logic if I don't have to.
commonMistakes: Salts the fact table but forgets to explode the dimension table, causing skewed-key rows to silently drop out of the join
Salts every row uniformly instead of only the known skewed key(s), unnecessarily inflating the join for normal data
Doesn't verify AQE's automatic skew join handling first before reaching for manual salting
Uses a salt bucket count too small to actually spread the hot key across enough partitions
Forgets to drop the salt column after the join, leaking an implementation detail into downstream schema
keyPoints: Salts only the known skewed key(s) on the fact side, leaving the rest of the data untouched
Explodes the dimension table to produce a matching row per salt bucket for the skewed key
Joins on the composite (customer_id, salt) key to preserve correctness
Recognizes this as the manual equivalent of AQE's automatic skew join handling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct salting logic applied selectively to the skewed key
Correctly explodes the dimension side to avoid dropping matched rows
Produces a correct, logically equivalent join result
Notes the AQE skew-join alternative/relationship

questions.title: Row-Level Security for a Shared Sales Table Across Regional Teams
questions.prompt: A shared catalog.sales.orders table in Unity Catalog needs to be visible to all five regional sales teams, but each region's analysts should only see their own region's rows -- and a separate exec_global group should see every row unmasked. Write the SQL to enforce this with a Unity Catalog row-level security view, without creating five separate physical tables.
questions.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW catalog.sales.orders_secure AS
SELECT *
FROM catalog.sales.orders
WHERE
  is_account_group_member('exec_global')
  OR region = (
    CASE
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_east')    THEN 'EAST'
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_west')    THEN 'WEST'
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_north')   THEN 'NORTH'
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_south')   THEN 'SOUTH'
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_central') THEN 'CENTRAL'
    END
  );

-- Lock down the base table so it can only be reached through the view
REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE catalog.sales.orders FROM `account users`;
GRANT SELECT ON VIEW catalog.sales.orders_secure TO `account users`;
questions.modelAnswer: is_account_group_member() is Unity Catalog's built-in function for checking the calling user's group membership at query time, which lets row-level security be expressed directly in SQL rather than in application code. The view's WHERE clause evaluates per-querying-user, not per-row-owner: exec_global always passes via the OR short-circuit regardless of region, while every other caller's rows are filtered by whichever single CASE branch matches their own group membership. Critically, this security guarantee only holds if the underlying base table itself isn't separately grantable -- if analysts retain direct SELECT on catalog.sales.orders, they can simply bypass the view and query the base table directly, seeing every row regardless of region. The REVOKE/GRANT pair isn't cleanup, it's the actual enforcement boundary; the view only provides security to the extent the base table is locked behind it. A user belonging to none of the listed groups and not in exec_global falls through the CASE to NULL, which matches no region and correctly returns zero rows rather than erroring. This same pattern generalizes to column masking by adding a similar CASE WHEN is_account_group_member(...) THEN real_column ELSE NULL END on sensitive columns within the same view.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I always flag when reviewing this kind of view is the REVOKE statement, because without it the whole thing is security theater -- anyone who still has SELECT on the base table just skips the view and sees everything, and that's an easy thing to miss in a review because the view itself looks completely correct. I'd also point out that the filtering logic runs based on who's asking the question, not any flag stored on the row itself, so the same physical table serves five different results depending on who's logged in -- that's the part that avoids needing five physical tables. And I'd double check the fallback case: if someone isn't in any of these groups, does the CASE return NULL cleanly, or does it error? We want a quiet zero rows, not a broken query, for a user who simply doesn't belong anywhere yet.
commonMistakes: Builds the secure view but leaves SELECT granted on the base table, so the row filtering is trivially bypassable
Writes the region-matching logic per-row-owner instead of per-querying-user's group membership
Doesn't handle the case of a user in none of the groups, risking an error instead of a safe zero-row result
Creates five physical per-region tables instead of one filtered view, duplicating storage and maintenance
Forgets exec_global needs an OR short-circuit, not just another CASE branch, to see all regions at once
keyPoints: Uses is_account_group_member() to filter rows based on the querying user's group at query time
Revokes direct SELECT on the base table so the view is the only access path
Handles the exec_global case as an OR condition granting unrestricted access
Avoids per-region physical table duplication by using one parameterized view

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct row-filtering logic using is_account_group_member()
Correctly revokes base table access to make the view the sole enforcement path
Correctly handles the exec_global unrestricted-access case
Avoids unnecessary physical table duplication

questions.title: Write a Lakeflow Pipeline Enforcing a Hard Quality Gate on Revenue Rows
questions.prompt: Using the incident from the earlier data-quality discussion -- negative revenue and null customer IDs reaching the gold layer -- write the actual Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline code for the silver table that enforces these as hard invariants, while quarantining a separate, recoverable issue (missing region code) instead of failing the pipeline over it.
questions.modelAnswer: expect_or_fail on valid_customer_id and non_negative_revenue encodes exactly the two conditions from the incident as hard invariants -- any batch containing a violating row causes this pipeline update to fail outright rather than letting even one bad row reach silver or gold, which is the correct severity for data that corrupts downstream financial aggregates: a single null customer_id breaking a join, or one negative revenue row skewing a sum, is not something to drop and move past silently. expect_or_drop on has_region_code treats missing region code as recoverable: rows failing that check are silently excluded from the output table, but still counted in the pipeline's event-log metrics, rather than failing the whole run -- appropriate because a missing region code is useful-but-not-critical dimension metadata, not something that corrupts a revenue total. All three expectations are evaluated per row during the same pipeline run, and their pass/fail/drop counts are visible in the Lakeflow pipeline's event log and UI graph, so the quarantine isn't invisible -- someone can still see how many rows were dropped for missing region code and decide whether that number warrants investigation. The severity choices here are proportionate to business impact: fail hard on invariants that corrupt the gold layer's numbers, quarantine-and-count everything else.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this incident-first: the whole point of this code is that the two things that actually went wrong last time -- null customer IDs and negative revenue -- get expect_or_fail, full stop, because those are exactly the rows that corrupt a financial number if they sneak through. Missing region code is a different kind of problem; it's annoying, not dangerous, so it gets expect_or_drop instead, which quietly excludes those rows but still counts them so we're not flying blind. I'd push back on anyone who wants to make everything expect_or_fail 'to be safe' -- that just means a non-critical field like region code starts taking down the whole pipeline, which trades one kind of incident for another.
commonMistakes: Uses expect_or_drop for the revenue/customer_id checks, silently losing exactly the rows the incident was about instead of failing loudly
Uses expect_or_fail for the region_code check, causing unnecessary pipeline failures over a non-critical field
Doesn't cast/validate the revenue column's type before checking it, letting a type issue masquerade as a data issue
Writes the expectation as a plain Python assert instead of the @dlt.expect_or_* decorator, losing event-log visibility into violations
Forgets that dropped rows from expect_or_drop still need to be monitored, not just silently discarded
keyPoints: Correctly maps hard invariants (null customer_id, negative revenue) to expect_or_fail
Correctly maps the recoverable issue (missing region code) to expect_or_drop
Explains why severity level should match business impact, not be applied uniformly
Notes that expectation outcomes remain visible via the pipeline event log/UI

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct expectation decorator and severity chosen for each condition
Correct, runnable Lakeflow pipeline code structure
Explains the reasoning behind severity choices tied to business impact
Notes observability of expectation outcomes

questions.title: A Reusable Terraform Module for Provisioning Fabric Capacity Across Dev, Test, and Prod
questions.prompt: Instead of three teams each hand-writing their own Terraform for a Fabric capacity (and inevitably drifting on SKU naming, tags, and admin assignment), write a reusable Terraform module that provisions a Fabric capacity, parameterized so dev/test/prod can call it with different SKUs while sharing identical structure.
questions.modelAnswer: The module encapsulates everything that should be identical across environments -- naming convention, tagging scheme, resource group pairing, admin group -- behind variables for the one thing that legitimately differs per environment, sku (and optionally admin_members if prod needs tighter membership). Each environment's root config becomes a short module call rather than a full copy of the resource definitions, so a structural fix, like a new required tag or a naming-convention change, is made once in the module and automatically applies to every environment on the next apply. That's the actual payoff over copy-pasted Terraform, which drifts the moment one environment's file gets hand-edited and the others don't. The naming pattern (fabric-cap-${var.environment}) guarantees every environment gets a distinct, predictable resource name without manual bookkeeping. Keeping state separate per environment -- separate state files or workspaces for dev/test/prod, implied here by the environments/ directory structure -- matters just as much, since a shared state file across environments means a prod apply could accidentally run against a plan computed against dev's state.
questions.professionalAnswer: When three teams are about to write near-identical Terraform, I'd stop them before they start and get the module written first, because the fix that matters here isn't 'provision a Fabric capacity,' it's 'make sure dev, test, and prod can never structurally drift from each other.' Everything that should be the same -- naming, tags, the admin group pattern -- lives in the module; the only thing each environment passes in is its SKU, maybe its admin list if prod needs to be locked down tighter. That way, if we ever need to add a required tag for cost tracking later, it's a one-line change in the module, not three separate PRs that might not all land the same way. I'd also make sure each environment has its own state file before anyone applies anything, because a shared state file across dev and prod is the kind of mistake you only make once.
commonMistakes: Copy-pastes the capacity resource block per environment instead of extracting a shared module
Hardcodes the SKU inside the module instead of parameterizing it
Shares one Terraform state file across all three environments, risking a dev change being applied to prod
Doesn't parameterize admin_members, giving every environment identical (often too-broad) admin access
Omits consistent tagging, making cost attribution/chargeback across environments unreliable later
keyPoints: Extracts a reusable module with environment and sku as the key variables
Keeps naming, tagging, and structure consistent across environments via the module
Separates state per environment to prevent cross-environment apply mistakes
Parameterizes admin membership rather than hardcoding identical access everywhere

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, reusable Terraform module structure
Correctly parameterizes the environment-specific differences (sku, admins)
Addresses state separation across environments
Consistent naming/tagging convention across environments

questions.title: Bringing a Manually Created Event Hub Under Bicep Management
questions.prompt: Six months ago, someone manually provisioned a production Event Hub namespace through the Azure Portal under time pressure. It's never been touched since, but now it needs to go through the same CI/CD-managed Bicep pipeline as everything else. Explain how you'd bring it under IaC management given Bicep/ARM doesn't have a true 'import' command like Terraform, and write the Bicep you'd use.
questions.modelAnswer: Bicep/ARM deployments are declarative and idempotent by name -- there's no separate 'import state' step like terraform import, because ARM doesn't track resource ownership the way Terraform's state file does. 'Importing' in practice means writing a Bicep resource block whose type, name, and properties exactly match the resource's CURRENT live configuration, then deploying it. Because ARM resolves a deployment by matching resource type and name, deploying a Bicep definition that matches an existing resource's current state is effectively a no-op update, and from that point forward the resource is 'under management' in the sense that the next deployment touching this Bicep file will apply diffs to it going forward. The critical risk is capturing the TRUE current configuration before writing that block -- if the manually-created Event Hub has settings (a specific capacity, a non-default retention, a particular throughput configuration) that get guessed wrong in the Bicep definition, the first deployment silently changes production instead of leaving it alone. The existing keyword resource reference is the safe way to read and confirm current properties before writing the managed resource block, rather than guessing. I'd also run a what-if deployment (az deployment group what-if) before the real apply specifically to confirm it reports zero or no-op changes, which is the actual verification that the Bicep definition genuinely matches reality.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd correct is the premise that we're looking for a terraform-import equivalent -- Bicep just doesn't work that way, since ARM doesn't keep a separate state file tracking what it owns. What actually happens is: we write a Bicep resource block that matches this Event Hub's current settings exactly, and the moment we deploy it and it comes back as a no-op, that resource is under management. The part I'd be most careful about is getting 'exactly' right -- I'd use the existing keyword first to read its real current config rather than guess at what someone set six months ago, and then I would not run this against production without a what-if deployment first. If what-if shows anything other than no changes, that's a sign my Bicep doesn't actually match reality yet, and I'd rather find that out from a dry run than from an unintended change to a live Event Hub.
commonMistakes: Assumes Bicep has a terraform import equivalent command and looks for one instead of writing a matching resource definition
Writes the Bicep resource block from assumed/default settings instead of verifying the resource's actual current configuration first
Skips a what-if deployment before the real apply, risking an unintended production change
Uses the existing keyword as if it brings the resource under management, when it's read-only and changes nothing
Doesn't account for properties that are immutable or hard to change needing to match exactly from day one
keyPoints: Explains ARM/Bicep has no stateful import; management starts by matching a resource's current live config in code
Uses the existing keyword to safely read current configuration before writing the managed definition
Verifies the match with a what-if deployment before the real apply
Flags the risk of a mismatched property causing an unintended change to production on first deploy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why Bicep has no true import and what bringing under management actually means
Correct use of the existing keyword to verify current state safely
Correctly matches the managed resource definition structure
Proposes what-if verification before the real deployment

questions.title: Enforcing Backward Compatibility on a Subject via the Schema Registry REST API
questions.prompt: Following the schema-governance redesign from the earlier incident, write the actual Schema Registry REST API calls your CI pipeline would run to (1) set a subject's compatibility mode to BACKWARD and (2) test a candidate schema against the current one before allowing a producer's CI build to merge.
questions.code:
# 1. Set BACKWARD compatibility on the subject (run once, or enforced via IaC)
curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json" \
  --data '{"compatibility": "BACKWARD"}' \
  http://schema-registry:8081/config/orders-value

# 2. In CI, before merging a producer change: test the candidate schema for compatibility
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json" \
  --data '{"schema": "{\"type\":\"record\",\"name\":\"Order\",\"fields\":[{\"name\":\"order_id\",\"type\":\"string\"},{\"name\":\"amount\",\"type\":\"double\"}]}"}' \
  http://schema-registry:8081/compatibility/subjects/orders-value/versions/latest

# Response: {"is_compatible": true} or {"is_compatible": false}
# CI should fail the build if is_compatible is false, before any registration happens
questions.modelAnswer: The /config/{subject} PUT endpoint sets the enforcement policy itself -- once set to BACKWARD, the registry will reject, at the /subjects/{subject}/versions registration endpoint, any new schema version that isn't backward-compatible with the latest registered version, which is the actual safety net. The /compatibility/subjects/{subject}/versions/latest POST endpoint used in CI is a separate dry-run test: calling it doesn't register anything, it just returns is_compatible true or false for the candidate schema against the current one, which is exactly what a CI pipeline needs -- check compatibility as a build gate before the producer's code, which would register the new schema at deploy time, ever merges. The key operational point is that this has to run in CI on every pull request that touches a schema file, not just be available as a manual command someone might remember to run, and the build should fail loudly on is_compatible: false with the response body surfaced in the CI log, so the engineer sees exactly what broke compatibility rather than a generic failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this as two different endpoints doing two different jobs, because mixing them up is the most common mistake I see. The /config endpoint is the policy switch -- flip it to BACKWARD once, and the registry itself now refuses any genuinely breaking schema at registration time, which is the real backstop. The /compatibility endpoint is what CI calls on every PR, and it's a dry run -- it tells you yes or no without registering anything, so you find out a change is breaking before it ever gets near deploy time. I'd insist this runs on every PR that touches a schema, not as an optional step, and I'd make sure the build output actually shows the registry's response, because 'compatibility check failed' with no detail sends an engineer hunting for a problem the API already described precisely.
commonMistakes: Confuses the /compatibility test endpoint with the /subjects registration endpoint, thinking compatibility testing registers a schema
Sets compatibility mode but never wires the /compatibility check into actual CI, leaving it manual/optional
Doesn't fail the CI build loudly on is_compatible: false, letting it merge anyway
Sets compatibility globally instead of per-subject, when different subjects may need different modes
Forgets this only protects the subject it's set on -- a renamed topic/subject starts with no compatibility mode by default
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes the /config (set policy) and /compatibility (dry-run test) endpoints
Wires the compatibility test into CI as a build gate, not a manual step
Fails the build and surfaces the response on incompatibility
Understands this is a per-subject setting, not global

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct REST API calls for setting compatibility mode and testing a candidate schema
Correctly distinguishes the dry-run test endpoint from registration
Describes correct CI gating behavior
Notes per-subject scoping of compatibility mode

questions.title: Configuring MirrorMaker 2 for Active/Passive Replication Between Two Data Centers
questions.prompt: Following the active/passive recommendation for the East/West DR design, write the MirrorMaker 2 connector configuration that replicates topics from the East (primary) cluster to the West (standby) cluster, including the settings that actually matter for a real failover drill -- not just basic topic mirroring.
questions.code:
# mm2.properties
clusters = east, west
east.bootstrap.servers = east-broker1:9092,east-broker2:9092
west.bootstrap.servers = west-broker1:9092,west-broker2:9092

east->west.enabled = true
west->east.enabled = false

# Replicate everything except internal topics
east->west.topics = orders.*, payments.*
east->west.topics.exclude = .*\.internal

# Sync consumer group offsets so failover can resume near the right position
east->west.emit.checkpoints.enabled = true
east->west.sync.group.offsets.enabled = true
checkpoints.topic.replication.factor = 3

# Preserve source partitioning / avoid renaming collisions
replication.policy.separator = .
east->west.replication.factor = 3

# Keep replication lag visible
east->west.emit.heartbeats.enabled = true
heartbeats.topic.replication.factor = 3
questions.modelAnswer: The directional flags, east->west.enabled = true and west->east.enabled = false, are what actually encode active/passive -- MM2 is bidirectionally capable, so leaving the reverse direction enabled by accident would create a replication loop or an unintended write path back into the primary, a common real-world misconfiguration. sync.group.offsets.enabled is the setting most teams skip and the one that determines whether failover is actually usable: without it, West has the replicated data but no translated consumer offsets, so a consumer failing over to West either reprocesses everything from the beginning or needs manual offset management. emit.checkpoints.enabled together with sync.group.offsets.enabled let MM2 periodically translate East's consumer offsets into West's offset space, so a failed-over consumer group can resume close to where it left off rather than from zero. emit.heartbeats.enabled gives an observable signal of replication health, specifically lag and whether replication is actually flowing, independent of whether any data happened to be produced recently, which matters for monitoring that the standby isn't silently stale. topics.exclude keeps MM2 from needlessly replicating its own internal/checkpoint topics. None of this is testable by configuration review alone -- the actual validation is running a failover drill: stop consuming from East, point consumers at West using the translated offsets, and measure how much, if any, reprocessing or data gap actually occurs, which is the RPO/RTO measurement the earlier design recommendation called for.
questions.professionalAnswer: The line I'd point to first in a review is west->east.enabled = false, because the single most common MirrorMaker mistake I see is leaving both directions on by accident and ending up with an unintended active/active loop when the intent was active/passive. The setting I'd insist on, though, is sync.group.offsets.enabled -- without it, this whole config replicates data beautifully and still leaves us with no usable failover, because our consumers would have no idea where to resume on West. And I'd tell the team configuring this alone doesn't prove anything -- the only way to know failover actually works is to run a real drill: stop consuming from East, flip to West, and measure exactly how much we reprocess or lose. That number is our real RPO, not whatever we assumed when we wrote this file.
commonMistakes: Enables both east->west and west->east, accidentally building an active/active loop instead of active/passive
Skips sync.group.offsets.enabled, leaving no path for consumers to resume cleanly on failover
Never actually runs a failover drill, treating 'replication is configured' as equivalent to 'failover works'
Doesn't exclude MM2's own internal/checkpoint/heartbeat topics from the replication topic list
Assumes topic names stay identical across clusters without accounting for replication.policy.separator renaming behavior
keyPoints: Correctly configures directional replication for active/passive (one direction only)
Enables checkpoint/offset sync so failover can resume without full reprocessing
Uses heartbeats to monitor replication health/lag independently of data flow
Recognizes configuration alone doesn't validate failover -- a drill is required

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct directional (active/passive) MM2 configuration
Correctly configures offset/checkpoint sync for usable failover
Includes replication health monitoring (heartbeats)
Notes the need for an actual failover drill to validate RPO/RTO

questions.title: Handling Late-Arriving Dimension Updates in a Fabric Warehouse With MERGE
questions.prompt: A customer dimension table in Fabric Warehouse is fed nightly from five regional source systems, and updates sometimes arrive a day or more late (a West region customer record corrected two days after the fact). Write the T-SQL MERGE statement that correctly applies these late-arriving updates as true upserts, including protecting against the batch accidentally reverting a customer record that a newer source batch already updated today.
questions.code:
MERGE INTO dbo.customer_dim AS target
USING staging.customer_updates AS source
    ON target.customer_id = source.customer_id
   AND target.region = source.region
WHEN MATCHED
     AND source.source_last_modified > target.source_last_modified
THEN UPDATE SET
    target.customer_name        = source.customer_name,
    target.email                = source.email,
    target.address              = source.address,
    target.source_last_modified = source.source_last_modified,
    target.updated_at           = SYSUTCDATETIME()
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET
THEN INSERT (customer_id, region, customer_name, email, address, source_last_modified, updated_at)
VALUES (source.customer_id, source.region, source.customer_name, source.email, source.address,
        source.source_last_modified, SYSUTCDATETIME());
questions.modelAnswer: The join predicate matches on the natural business key, customer_id plus region, not a surrogate or batch key, so a two-day-late correction for the same customer still finds and targets the right existing row rather than inserting a duplicate. The critical guard is the AND source.source_last_modified > target.source_last_modified condition on the WHEN MATCHED clause -- without it, a plain MERGE applies whatever's in the incoming batch unconditionally, so a stale, two-day-late batch for a customer that a same-day newer batch already corrected would silently overwrite the newer, correct data with the older, late-arriving data, which is exactly the accidental revert the prompt asks to protect against. This requires carrying a source_last_modified, or equivalent business timestamp from the source system rather than the ETL load timestamp, through to the target table specifically so this comparison is possible -- a load_date/updated_at column alone can only answer 'which batch run touched this row most recently,' not 'which version of the actual customer record is newer,' which is the wrong question here. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET handles the simple new-customer insert case without any conditional, since there's nothing to compare against yet.
questions.professionalAnswer: The line I'd point to first when reviewing this is the condition on WHEN MATCHED, because a plain MERGE without it is a trap waiting to happen with five regional sources and late-arriving data -- it'll run fine for months until the day a two-day-late batch for a customer we already corrected today silently reverts that correction, and nobody notices until someone asks why a customer's address changed back to something wrong. The fix is comparing against the source system's own last-modified timestamp, not when our ETL happened to load the row, because those answer two completely different questions. I'd also double-check the join key includes region, not just customer_id, since five regional systems feeding one table is exactly the setup where an ID collision across regions would otherwise merge two different customers into one row.
commonMistakes: Writes a plain MERGE without the source_last_modified comparison, letting late-arriving stale data overwrite newer corrections
Compares against the target's load/ETL timestamp instead of a true source-system business timestamp
Joins only on customer_id without region, causing cross-region collisions if IDs aren't globally unique
Doesn't handle WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET, silently dropping genuinely new customers
Updates source_last_modified unconditionally even in the insert branch without carrying the source's actual timestamp
keyPoints: Joins on the correct natural business key for the dimension (customer_id + region)
Guards the UPDATE branch with a true source-timestamp comparison to prevent reverting newer data
Distinguishes a business/source timestamp from an ETL load timestamp
Correctly handles the insert branch for genuinely new customers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct MERGE structure with appropriate join key
Correctly guards against reverting newer data using a source timestamp comparison
Distinguishes source timestamp from ETL load timestamp in the explanation
Correctly handles the insert case for new rows

questions.title: Setting Up Locked Remote State for Terraform Across Multiple Data Platform Teams
questions.prompt: Three data platform teams (Databricks infra, Fabric infra, Kafka infra) are about to start running Terraform against shared Azure infrastructure from their own laptops and separate CI pipelines. Without any coordination so far, there's an obvious risk of two applies racing and corrupting state. Write the Terraform backend configuration that gives each team properly locked, isolated remote state, and explain what would happen without the locking piece.
questions.modelAnswer: The azurerm backend's blob storage natively supports state locking via a blob lease -- when any terraform plan or apply starts, Terraform acquires a lease on the specific blob at that key, and any other concurrent terraform run against the same key blocks or errors out until the lease is released, which is the actual mechanism preventing two concurrent applies from corrupting the same state file. Isolation between the three teams comes from using a distinct key per team within the same storage account and container -- Kafka infra's apply only ever locks kafka-infra/terraform.tfstate, so it can run fully in parallel with Databricks infra's apply against a different key with zero contention, while all three still benefit from one centrally managed, access-controlled storage account rather than three separately administered ones. Without locking, for example if state were kept locally or on a backend that doesn't support lease semantics, two simultaneous applies reading the same state, computing a plan, and writing back create a classic race: whichever apply finishes last silently overwrites the other's recorded state, so Terraform's own record of what exists in Azure no longer matches reality. The next plan run then proposes to 'fix' resources that are actually fine, or fails to detect resources the other apply genuinely created, and manual state surgery becomes the only way out.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before these three teams run a single apply, I'd get each of them onto a distinct state key in the same shared storage account -- same account for central management and access control, but kafka-infra, fabric-infra, and databricks-infra never touch each other's state file, so their applies can run fully in parallel without any risk of collision. The locking piece is what actually stops two people on the same team from racing each other on the same key -- Terraform grabs a blob lease the moment an apply starts, and a second apply against that same key just waits or fails until the first one releases it. If I skipped that, the failure mode isn't abstract -- it's two applies both reading the same state, both computing a plan from it, and whichever one finishes last just overwrites the other's result, so Terraform's own record of what's actually in Azure goes stale, and the next person to run a plan gets confusing, wrong diffs with no obvious explanation.
commonMistakes: Puts all three teams' state in a single shared key/file instead of distinct keys per team
Assumes any remote backend provides locking automatically, without confirming it actually supports lease-based locking
Doesn't restrict storage account access control, leaving all three teams with blanket write access to each other's state
Treats state locking as solving merge conflicts in the Terraform code itself, which it doesn't -- only concurrent apply races
Keeps state locally on a laptop for 'just this one change,' bypassing the shared backend and locking entirely
keyPoints: Uses a shared remote backend (azurerm) with a distinct state key per team
Explains blob lease as the actual locking mechanism preventing concurrent apply corruption
Describes the concrete failure mode of unlocked concurrent applies (state overwritten, drift undetected)
Separates team isolation (distinct keys) from the locking guarantee (per-key lease)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct backend configuration with per-team state key isolation
Correctly explains the locking mechanism (blob lease)
Correctly describes the failure mode without locking
Addresses access control alongside locking

questions.title: Unity Catalog Cross-Workspace Access Fails After a Metastore Split
questions.prompt: Your company runs three Databricks workspaces attached to a single Unity Catalog metastore in East US. After a platform team migrates one workspace to a new region for latency reasons, analysts in that workspace suddenly get 'PERMISSION_DENIED: metastore does not exist for this workspace' errors on tables that worked fine the day before, while the other two workspaces are unaffected. Diagnose the root cause and describe the correct fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A Unity Catalog metastore is a region-scoped object — exactly one metastore can be assigned per region per account, and a workspace can only attach to a metastore that lives in the same region as the workspace itself. When the platform team moved the workspace to a new region, the workspace's metastore assignment did not silently follow it; Databricks either detached the workspace from its original metastore or left it pointing at an assignment that is now cross-region and therefore invalid, which is exactly what produces the 'metastore does not exist for this workspace' error — it is not a permissions bug on any table, grant, or catalog, it is that the workspace has no valid, region-matched metastore assignment at all, so every object underneath that metastore becomes unreachable from that workspace regardless of the ACLs on it. The fix is to either provision or identify a Unity Catalog metastore that already exists in the new region and explicitly re-assign the migrated workspace to it, or, if the organization wants a single logical catalog of data rather than duplicated metastores, to use Delta Sharing to publish the relevant catalog's tables from the original region's metastore to the new workspace instead of trying to force a same-metastore attachment across regions, which Unity Catalog does not support. Before doing either, the team should audit whether any table/view definitions, external locations, or storage credentials referenced a region-specific path, since those will also need re-pointing. The deeper governance lesson is that metastore assignment should be treated as an immutable constraint during any workspace relocation planning, not an afterthought discovered via a production incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd explain this to the platform team is: you didn't break any grants, you broke the geography. A Unity Catalog metastore is pinned to a region, one per region per account, and a workspace can only ever attach to the metastore sitting in its own region — so the moment you moved that workspace to a new region, its old metastore attachment became invalid, and that error message is Databricks telling you exactly that, even though it reads like a permissions problem. My first move is to confirm there's no metastore provisioned yet in the new region, then decide: do we stand one up and re-assign the workspace to it, or do we keep this workspace reading from the original metastore's catalogs via Delta Sharing instead of forcing a direct attachment that the platform doesn't support. I'd also flag that this should never have shipped as a surprise — workspace relocation needs a pre-flight checklist that calls out metastore region-matching explicitly, because this exact failure mode is completely predictable once you know the constraint.
commonMistakes: Treats the error as a grants/ACL problem and starts re-running GRANT statements on the affected tables
Assumes the metastore 'moved with' the workspace automatically during region migration
Tries to attach the relocated workspace directly to the original region's metastore, not realizing cross-region attachment is unsupported
Doesn't check whether external locations/storage credentials also need re-pointing after the fix
Jumps to provisioning a new metastore without first considering Delta Sharing as a lighter-weight alternative
keyPoints: Identifies metastore-to-region binding as the root cause, not a permissions issue
Recognizes a workspace can only attach to a metastore in its own region
Proposes either provisioning/assigning a region-matched metastore or using Delta Sharing
Checks for region-specific external locations/storage credentials needing updates
Recommends region-matching become a pre-flight step for future workspace relocations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses metastore region-binding as root cause
Rules out grants/ACLs as the actual problem with sound reasoning
Proposes a valid fix (region-matched metastore or Delta Sharing)
Addresses downstream concerns (external locations, process improvement)

questions.title: A Lakeflow Pipeline Is Silently Dropping Records
questions.prompt: A Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline that ingests order events has been running green for three weeks with no failed runs, but a downstream finance reconciliation job discovers that roughly 2% of source records never made it into the target Delta table. There are no pipeline errors, no failed flows, and the run metrics show 'success.' Diagnose how this could happen and what you'd change.
questions.modelAnswer: A pipeline reporting success while silently losing rows is almost always an expectations configuration issue: Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines let you attach data-quality expectations to a flow with three distinct enforcement modes — warn (log the violation but keep the row), drop (discard the violating row but keep the pipeline green), and fail (stop the pipeline on violation). If an expectation such as a null check or a referential constraint was set to drop instead of fail, every row that violates it is quietly removed from the output and counted in the pipeline's own metrics as 'dropped by expectation,' which does not surface as a run failure because, by design, it isn't one — the pipeline did exactly what it was told to do. The reason nobody caught it for three weeks is that 'success' status and 'dropped record count' are two different signals, and the team was almost certainly only watching the former. The fix starts with checking the pipeline's event log / data quality metrics tab for the specific expectation and its violation count — that will show precisely which rows and why. Then the team needs to decide, with the business, whether those specific rows genuinely are bad data that should be dropped (in which case drop is correct but needs active monitoring and alerting on the drop count, not silent tolerance), or whether the expectation is too strict or miscoded and should be loosened or changed to fail so bad upstream data gets caught immediately instead of silently vanishing. Longer term, any expectation using drop in a financially sensitive pipeline should have an explicit alert threshold wired to its violation metric, because 'green pipeline' cannot be the only signal anyone is watching when correctness, not just availability, is the actual requirement.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'the pipeline isn't lying, it's just not telling you the whole story' problem. In Lakeflow, expectations have three modes, and drop is the quiet one — it strips out violating rows but still reports the run as a success, because from the pipeline's point of view it succeeded at doing exactly what you configured. So my first stop isn't the run logs, it's the data-quality metrics panel for that pipeline, where the actual drop counts per expectation live. Once I find which expectation is eating 2% of rows, the real conversation is with finance and whoever owns the source system: is dropping those rows actually correct, or did someone configure drop when they meant fail? If drop is genuinely the right call, fine, but it can't go unmonitored in a pipeline feeding financial reconciliation — I'd wire an alert on that specific violation count so a silent 2% doesn't become a silent 10% next quarter. The bigger fix is cultural: 'pipeline succeeded' and 'pipeline produced correct, complete output' are two different claims, and this incident is what happens when a team only ever checks the first one.
commonMistakes: Assumes a 'success' pipeline run guarantees complete data and looks elsewhere (source system, network) for missing rows
Doesn't know Lakeflow expectations have distinct warn/drop/fail modes with different observability implications
Finds the dropped rows but doesn't check whether drop vs. fail is actually the business-correct choice
Fixes this one expectation but doesn't audit other expectations in the same or other pipelines for the same silent-drop risk
Proposes alerting on pipeline failure status instead of on the violation/drop-count metric itself
keyPoints: Identifies expectations' drop mode as the likely silent-loss mechanism
Distinguishes 'pipeline succeeded' from 'pipeline output is complete/correct'
Locates the actual violation counts via pipeline data-quality metrics, not just run status
Evaluates whether drop vs. fail is the business-correct enforcement mode here
Proposes alerting on violation/drop counts, not just on run failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies drop-mode expectations as root cause
Explains why this is invisible to standard success/failure monitoring
Proposes locating and reviewing the specific violation metrics
Proposes a durable monitoring/alerting fix

questions.title: Databricks Job Cluster Costs Spike 10x Overnight
questions.prompt: Your Databricks cost dashboard shows DBU consumption jumped roughly 10x overnight with no new workload launched by anyone on the team, and finance is asking for an explanation before the month closes. Walk through how you'd investigate this and what you'd expect to find.
questions.modelAnswer: A sudden 10x overnight spike with no new workload points to one of a small number of mechanisms, and the investigation should rule them in or out in order of likelihood rather than guessing. First, pull the account's cluster event logs and billable usage system tables (system.billing.usage) filtered to the spike window, grouped by cluster and job, to see which specific compute resource actually drove the jump — this turns 'costs spiked' into 'cluster X ran for 14 hours instead of its normal 20 minutes.' The most common root causes at this signature are: a runaway autoscaling job where a bad join or skewed partition caused the cluster to scale to its max node count and stay pinned there without actually making progress; a job whose cluster was configured without an automatic termination timeout, so it kept running (and billing) long after the job's actual work finished or failed; or a zombie all-purpose cluster that someone left running interactively and forgot, accumulating idle DBU-hours at full size overnight. Each has a distinct signature in the event log: autoscaling-to-max with flat progress looks very different from a cluster sitting idle at a fixed size for hours. Once the specific cluster and cause are identified, the immediate fix is to terminate it and look at whether a cluster policy would have prevented this — enforcing a max node count, requiring auto-termination after N minutes of idle time, and restricting interactive all-purpose clusters from running unattended overnight are all policy-level guardrails, not one-off fixes. For the finance conversation, the answer needs to be the specific mechanism and dollar amount, plus the policy change that makes this structurally harder to repeat — not just 'we turned off a cluster.'
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I say anything to finance, I want the actual billing data, not a guess — so I'm pulling system.billing.usage filtered to the spike window and grouping by cluster to find exactly which compute resource drove the number up tenfold. In my experience this is almost always one of three things: a job that autoscaled to its ceiling and got stuck there churning on a bad join, a cluster with no auto-termination timeout that just kept running after the actual work was done, or an all-purpose cluster someone left running interactively overnight. Whichever it is, I want to be able to tell finance the specific story — 'cluster X ran for 14 hours instead of 20 minutes because of a skewed join' — rather than a vague apology. And the fix I bring back isn't just killing that one cluster; it's a cluster policy that caps max nodes and forces auto-termination, because the actual failure here is that nothing was stopping a misbehaving job from running up an unbounded bill, and that's a policy gap, not a one-off mistake by whoever launched the job.
commonMistakes: Speculates about the cause without pulling actual billing/usage system table data first
Doesn't distinguish between autoscaling-to-max-with-no-progress vs. simple idle/forgotten cluster — different root causes, different fixes
Fixes the one cluster but doesn't propose a cluster policy to prevent recurrence
Doesn't consider that a missing auto-termination timeout is often the simplest and most common cause
Reports the dollar impact to finance without identifying the specific mechanism
keyPoints: Uses system.billing.usage / cluster event logs to find the specific resource responsible
Distinguishes runaway autoscaling, missing auto-termination, and zombie interactive clusters as distinct causes
Connects root cause to a specific, verifiable story (which cluster, how long, why)
Proposes cluster policies (max nodes, auto-termination) as the durable fix
Separates the immediate incident fix from the structural prevention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes concrete investigation using billing/usage data
Correctly enumerates plausible root-cause mechanisms
Proposes cluster policy guardrails as the durable fix
Frames findings in terms finance/stakeholders can act on

questions.title: Shared Fabric Capacity Throttles Across Unrelated Workspaces
questions.prompt: Your organization runs 12 business-unit workspaces on a single shared Fabric F64 capacity. On the last business day of the quarter, a finance team's heavy Spark notebook job causes Direct Lake reports in three completely unrelated marketing workspaces to start returning throttling errors and slow refreshes. Explain the mechanism behind this and how you'd both resolve the immediate incident and prevent a repeat.
questions.modelAnswer: Fabric capacity is a single shared pool of compute units (CUs) measured against smoothed, rolling 24-hour and burst consumption, and every workload across every workspace assigned to that capacity — Spark jobs, Direct Lake queries, dataflows, pipelines — draws from the same pool. There is no per-workspace isolation inside a single capacity: a heavy Spark job in finance's workspace consumes CUs exactly as if it were running in marketing's workspace, because as far as the capacity's throttling logic is concerned, there is no 'finance' or 'marketing,' only aggregate consumption against that F64's limits. When consumption exceeds the smoothed threshold, Fabric enforces interactive delay and then rejection-level throttling across the entire capacity, not just the workload that caused it — which is exactly why unrelated marketing reports started failing. The immediate fix is to identify the offending job via the capacity metrics app, which breaks down consumption by item and workspace, confirm finance's notebook as the driver, and either kill/reschedule it off-hours or temporarily scale the capacity up (F64 to F128, which Fabric supports as a near-instantaneous SKU change) to absorb the burst. The durable prevention is architectural: either move heavy, bursty workloads like finance's quarter-end Spark job onto their own dedicated capacity so they can't starve other business units, or establish workload scheduling windows and per-workspace consumption alerting so a single team's spike is caught and throttled by policy before it becomes a capacity-wide incident. A single shared capacity across 12 business units without any isolation or chargeback visibility is itself the design smell this incident is surfacing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd explain to the marketing team first is that this isn't a bug in their reports — a Fabric capacity is one shared bucket of compute units, and there's no wall between workspaces inside it, so finance's heavy Spark job and marketing's Direct Lake queries were always drawing from the exact same pool. When finance's quarter-end job spiked consumption past the smoothed threshold, Fabric throttles the whole capacity, not just the workload responsible, so marketing paid the price for a job they didn't even know existed. For the immediate fix, I'm in the capacity metrics app finding the actual offending item, and if it's genuinely a one-time burst, scaling the SKU up temporarily is the fastest relief valve. But the conversation I actually want to have afterward is about whether 12 business units belong on one shared capacity at all without any isolation — if finance is going to keep running bursty quarter-end jobs, they probably need their own dedicated capacity, and either way we need per-workspace consumption visibility so the next spike gets caught by an alert instead of by marketing's Slack channel.

Doesn't know Fabric capacity throttling is smoothed/aggregate across all workspaces on that capacity, not per-workspace
Fixes the immediate incident (scaling up) without addressing the lack of workload isolation
Doesn't use the capacity metrics app to identify which specific item/workspace drove the spike
Proposes splitting workspaces without proposing any consumption monitoring/alerting

Identifies the offending workload via the capacity metrics app
Proposes immediate relief (scale SKU up, reschedule/kill the job)

Frames the shared-capacity-for-12-business-units setup as the underlying design gap

questions.title: A Kafka Consumer Group Spirals Into a Rebalance Storm After Failover
questions.prompt: After a datacenter failover, a critical Kafka consumer group with 24 consumers across 8 pods gets stuck cycling through rebalances every 30-60 seconds for over an hour, and lag climbs continuously even though the pods all report healthy. Diagnose what's likely happening and how you'd stabilize it.
questions.modelAnswer: A rebalance storm after a failover almost always traces to the session/heartbeat and max-poll-interval settings interacting badly with a sudden load or latency change, rather than any single consumer actually being unhealthy. The most likely mechanism: after failover, brokers or network paths changed, so poll latency or processing time per batch increased for some consumers; if a consumer's processing time between polls exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, the broker's group coordinator considers it dead and evicts it, triggering a rebalance — but the consumer itself never crashed, so it rejoins, triggers another rebalance to get repartitioned, and if its processing is still too slow under the new conditions, it gets evicted again, producing exactly the 30-60 second cycling observed. Each rebalance also pauses the entire group's consumption (classic eager rebalancing stops all partition assignment during the protocol), which is why lag climbs continuously — the group spends more time rebalancing than actually consuming. The fix has an immediate and a structural layer. Immediately: check consumer logs for 'Attempt to heartbeat failed since group is rebalancing' and 'member sent heartbeat but is marked as leaving' patterns to confirm this specific cause, then either reduce batch processing time per poll (smaller max.poll.records) or raise max.poll.interval.ms to give slower post-failover processing enough headroom to complete without eviction. Structurally, migrating to incremental cooperative rebalancing (the CooperativeStickyAssignor) prevents full-group stop-the-world rebalances, since it reassigns only the partitions that actually need to move rather than revoking every partition from every consumer on each rebalance — this alone would have kept the other partitions consuming throughout the incident instead of stalling the whole group.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I'd tell the incident channel first is: nobody's actually crashed, this is a rebalance loop, and the usual cause after a failover is that something got slower — network hop, broker response time, whatever — and now some consumers are taking longer between polls than max.poll.interval.ms allows, so the coordinator keeps kicking them out and triggering a rebalance, they rejoin, and if they're still slow, they get kicked again. That's your 30-60 second cycle. I'd grep consumer logs for heartbeat-failed-during-rebalance messages to confirm it, then buy headroom immediately by either raising max.poll.interval.ms or shrinking max.poll.records so each poll cycle finishes faster. But the fix I actually want to land afterward is switching this group to the cooperative sticky assignor instead of the default eager one, because eager rebalancing stops every partition in the group on every rebalance — which is exactly why lag climbed even on the consumers that were fine. Cooperative rebalancing only reassigns what actually needs to move, so a bad apple doesn't stall the whole barrel next time.
commonMistakes: Assumes consumer pods are actually crashing/restarting rather than being evicted and rejoining
Doesn't connect increased post-failover latency to max.poll.interval.ms eviction
Doesn't recognize eager rebalancing pauses the entire group, explaining why healthy consumers also show rising lag
Jumps to restarting pods or scaling consumers without diagnosing the actual eviction loop
Doesn't propose the cooperative sticky assignor as the structural fix
keyPoints: Diagnoses eviction due to exceeding max.poll.interval.ms, not consumer crashes
Explains why lag climbs even on healthy consumers (eager rebalancing stops the whole group)
Confirms via consumer log patterns (heartbeat/rebalance messages)
Proposes immediate relief (poll interval/batch size tuning)
Proposes cooperative sticky assignor as the structural fix to avoid stop-the-world rebalances

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the eviction-rejoin rebalance loop mechanism
Explains why healthy consumers' lag also rises (eager rebalance)
Proposes correct immediate mitigation
