questions.title: A Breaking Schema Change Takes Down Six Downstream Consumers at Once
questions.prompt: A producer team pushes a change to an Avro schema for the orders topic that renames a required field, and within minutes six downstream consumer applications start throwing deserialization exceptions. The schema registry is running in backward-compatibility mode. Explain how this got through, and design both the immediate fix and a process change to prevent it.
questions.modelAnswer: Backward compatibility mode checks whether consumers using the NEW schema can read data written with the OLD schema — it does not check the reverse, so it offers no protection against a change that breaks consumers who are still running the OLD schema against newly-produced data, which is exactly what happened here. Renaming a required field is, under Avro's semantics, a genuinely breaking change unless the old field name is preserved as an alias: without a matching alias, a consumer deserializing with the prior schema has no mapping for the incoming field and fails outright. Critically, backward compatibility checking would have flagged this as incompatible and rejected the registration at the registry if it had been enforced correctly — so the real question is whether compatibility checking was actually set to a mode and enforcement level that should have caught this (e.g., someone used FORWARD or NONE instead of BACKWARD, or compatibility checks were bypassed via a force-register flag), because a correctly-configured BACKWARD-compatible registry should never have accepted a field rename without an alias in the first place. The immediate fix is to roll back the schema registration to the previous version (registries support this) so existing consumers resume working, then have the producer team add the rename as an alias-preserving change or, better, add the new field name without removing the old one and run both in parallel during a deprecation window. The process fix is to require schema changes to go through a CI check that calls the registry's compatibility-check API before merge, not at production-push time, and to adopt a stricter default compatibility mode like FULL (requiring both backward and forward compatibility) for shared, multi-consumer topics like orders, since backward-only is not sufficient protection when a dozen independent teams consume the same topic.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clarify for the team, because it's the actual root cause here, is that 'backward compatible' doesn't mean 'safe for everyone' — it means new-schema consumers can read old data, not that old-schema consumers can survive new data, and a field rename without an alias breaks exactly the direction backward compatibility doesn't check. So either the registry wasn't actually enforcing BACKWARD mode correctly, or someone force-pushed past the check, because a properly enforced backward-compatible registry should have rejected this rename outright. Immediate move: roll the schema registration back to the previous version so the six consumers recover right away, then tell the producer team the rename needs to come back as an additive change — new field alongside the old one, deprecate on a timeline, never a same-release rename. Longer term, I don't want compatibility checking happening implicitly at push time at all; I want it gated in CI before merge, and for a shared topic like orders with a dozen consumers, I'd push for FULL compatibility as the default, not backward-only, because backward-only clearly wasn't enough protection for a topic this widely consumed.
commonMistakes: Assumes 'backward compatible' mode would have caught any breaking change, without understanding its directionality
Doesn't recognize a field rename needs an alias to be non-breaking under Avro semantics
Fixes the immediate outage (rollback) without investigating why the registry allowed the change through
Proposes no CI-level gating, leaving the same bypass possible next time
Doesn't consider upgrading to FULL compatibility for a widely-shared topic
keyPoints: Explains backward-compatibility directionality correctly (new schema reads old data, not vice versa)
Identifies the rename-without-alias as the specific breaking change
Investigates why the registry check didn't block the change (misconfigured mode or bypass)
Proposes rollback as immediate fix and additive/alias-based change as the correct producer fix
Proposes CI-gated compatibility checks and stricter (FULL) mode for shared topics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains backward-compatibility semantics and why this slipped through
Proposes correct immediate recovery action
Proposes correct producer-side fix (additive/alias, not rename)
Proposes process fix: CI gating and/or stricter compatibility mode

questions.title: Terraform State Lock Blocks Two Teams' Deploys for an Hour
questions.prompt: Two platform teams share a single Terraform state file for a Fabric capacity and its related Azure resources. A CI pipeline deploy from one team crashes mid-apply, leaving a DynamoDB/Azure state lock held, and a second team's urgent hotfix deploy is now blocked for over an hour with no clear owner of the stuck lock. Diagnose the situation and describe both the safe recovery and the architectural change you'd propose.
questions.modelAnswer: Terraform's state locking exists to prevent two concurrent applies from corrupting the same state file through a race condition, and it is working exactly as designed here — the problem is that the process holding the lock died (CI pipeline crash) without releasing it, which is a known failure mode of any lock implementation: the lock has no automatic expiry tied to process liveness unless the backend specifically supports lock-breaking with a timeout. The safe recovery is not to force-unlock blindly; the engineer must first confirm the crashed apply did not leave the actual infrastructure in a partially-applied, inconsistent state, by checking the crashed pipeline's logs for how far the apply got and cross-checking actual resource state in Azure against what Terraform's last-known state file believes exists. Once confirmed the underlying resources are consistent (or reconciled), terraform force-unlock <lock-id> can safely release the stuck lock, after which the second team's apply can proceed; force-unlocking without that verification risks a corrupted state file if the original apply is, in fact, still silently running somewhere. The deeper architectural issue is that two independent teams sharing one monolithic state file for related-but-separable resources (a Fabric capacity plus its Azure plumbing) creates exactly this blast radius — one team's crash blocks the other team's unrelated urgent work. The fix is to split state by team/component boundary using separate state files (or Terraform workspaces/modules with independent backends) so a lock or corruption in one team's state cannot block another team's deploy, combined with CI pipeline safeguards — a deploy timeout that automatically triggers a lock-release-and-alert workflow instead of leaving a stuck lock for a human to discover an hour later.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd say in the incident channel: don't force-unlock yet. The lock mechanism did its job — it stopped a second apply from racing a first one — the actual problem is the first apply crashed without cleaning up after itself, which is a known gap in how most locking backends work. Before I touch the lock, I want to know how far that crashed apply actually got, because if it's still silently running or left infrastructure half-applied, force-unlocking and running a second apply on top of that is how you actually corrupt state. Once I've confirmed actual Azure resource state matches what Terraform's state file believes, force-unlock is safe and the hotfix can go through. But the conversation I want to have right after the fire's out is: why do two teams share one state file for resources that don't really need to be coupled? I'd split this into per-team or per-component state files so one team's crashed pipeline can never again hold the other team's urgent deploy hostage, and I'd add a deploy timeout to CI that automatically flags and alerts on a stuck lock instead of letting it sit silently for an hour before someone notices.
commonMistakes: Force-unlocks immediately without verifying the crashed apply's actual progress against real infrastructure state
Treats the lock itself as the bug, rather than the crash-without-cleanup failure mode it's protecting against
Fixes the immediate incident without addressing the shared-state architectural coupling
Doesn't propose CI-level safeguards (timeout/alerting) to catch stuck locks faster next time
Assumes splitting state is purely an organizational preference rather than an actual blast-radius reduction
keyPoints: Explains locking is working correctly; the gap is crash-without-release, not the lock mechanism itself
Verifies actual resource state before force-unlocking to avoid state corruption
Uses terraform force-unlock only after that verification
Proposes splitting shared state by team/component boundary to reduce blast radius
Proposes CI-level deploy timeout/alerting for stuck locks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses crash-without-release as the mechanism, not the lock design
Describes safe verification before force-unlocking
Proposes splitting state to reduce blast radius
Proposes CI safeguards against recurrence

questions.title: Exactly-Once Semantics Quietly Break After a Kafka Transactional Producer Restart
questions.prompt: A Kafka Streams application configured with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 is restarted after a crash, and a downstream audit discovers a small number of duplicate records in the output topic — something the team believed exactly-once guarantees should have prevented entirely. Diagnose how duplicates could still appear and what you'd check.
questions.modelAnswer: Exactly-once semantics in Kafka guarantee that a transactional producer's writes across its input offset commits and output records are atomic — either the whole set of writes for a transaction commits or none of it does — but that guarantee is scoped to the Kafka cluster boundary and to records produced through the same transactional producer with a consistent transactional.id. The most common ways duplicates still appear despite exactly_once_v2 being configured are: first, if any part of the pipeline writes to a non-Kafka sink (a database, an external API call, a side effect inside a transform) as part of processing a record, that write is entirely outside Kafka's transactional boundary and will be re-executed on reprocessing after a crash, since Kafka can only guarantee exactly-once for the Kafka-to-Kafka portion of the pipeline, not external side effects; second, if the transactional.id was not held stable across the restart — for instance if it's generated dynamically per-instance rather than being a stable per-partition identity — the producer may be treated as a new transactional session rather than resuming the prior one, which breaks the fencing mechanism that prevents zombie-producer duplicate writes; third, if the consumer reading the output topic downstream is itself not read_committed (isolation.level=read_committed), it will read uncommitted/aborted transactional records that later got rolled back, appearing as duplicates or phantom data. The investigation should check all three in order: confirm whether any non-Kafka side effects exist in the topology, confirm transactional.id generation is stable and partition-scoped across restarts, and confirm every downstream consumer explicitly sets read_committed rather than relying on the (non-transactional) default read_uncommitted behavior for non-Streams consumers.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd push back on gently is the assumption baked into 'exactly-once should have prevented this entirely' — Kafka's exactly-once guarantee is scoped to Kafka-to-Kafka writes inside the transactional boundary, it is not a blanket guarantee over the whole pipeline. So my first question is whether this topology has any side effect outside Kafka — a database write, an API call — because those happen outside the transaction and will absolutely replay on restart no matter how correctly exactly_once_v2 is configured. If there's nothing external, my next check is the transactional.id: it has to be stable and partition-scoped across restarts for Kafka's producer fencing to actually resume the same transactional identity instead of starting a new one, which is a surprisingly easy thing to get wrong if it's generated per-process-start instead of per-partition. And last, I'd check every downstream consumer's isolation.level — if anything reading that output topic is sitting on the default read_uncommitted instead of explicit read_committed, it's going to see aborted transactional writes as if they were real, which looks exactly like a duplicate. Exactly-once is a precise, scoped guarantee, and duplicates usually mean something fell just outside that scope, not that the guarantee itself failed.
commonMistakes: Assumes exactly_once_v2 is a blanket guarantee across the entire pipeline including non-Kafka side effects
Doesn't check for external (non-Kafka) writes inside the processing topology as the likely real cause
Doesn't know transactional.id must remain stable/partition-scoped across restarts for fencing to work correctly
Doesn't check downstream consumers' isolation.level, assuming read_committed is the default everywhere
Treats this as a Kafka bug rather than a scoping/configuration issue
keyPoints: Explains exactly-once is scoped to Kafka-to-Kafka transactional writes, not external side effects
Identifies non-Kafka side effects in the topology as a primary duplicate source
Checks transactional.id stability across restarts for correct producer fencing
Checks downstream consumers' isolation.level (read_committed vs. default read_uncommitted)
Correctly frames this as a scoping issue, not a Kafka guarantee failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the scope of Kafka exactly-once guarantees
Identifies external side effects as a likely duplicate source
Checks transactional.id stability/fencing across restarts
Checks downstream consumer isolation.level

questions.title: A Direct Lake Semantic Model Silently Falls Back to Import Mode
questions.prompt: A Fabric semantic model built on Direct Lake has been serving fast, low-latency reports for months. After a routine upsert pattern change in the underlying Lakehouse pipeline, the BI team notices report refreshes suddenly take minutes instead of being near-instant, and data feels 'stale' until a manual refresh. Diagnose what likely happened and how you'd confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer: The symptom pattern — Direct Lake was fast and near-instant, then suddenly behaves like a slow, manually-refreshed import model — is the signature of a Direct Lake to Direct Lake-with-fallback-to-Import transition, which Fabric performs automatically and silently when it determines the underlying Delta table no longer meets Direct Lake's requirements for direct, in-place reading. The most common trigger after a pipeline change is a shift in how the Lakehouse pipeline performs upserts: if the new pattern produces a very high number of small Parquet files per Delta table (for example, row-by-row or micro-batch merges without any compaction step), the table can exceed Direct Lake's practical limits on file/row-group fragmentation, or if the pipeline change introduced a data type Direct Lake doesn't support directly, or pushed a table past certain size guardrails for the capacity's SKU, Fabric falls back to importing the data into the semantic model's own cache instead of reading the Delta files directly — which explains both the slowdown (it's now doing a real import/refresh) and the staleness (it only updates data on that scheduled or manual refresh, not continuously like true Direct Lake). To confirm, the first place to check is the semantic model's refresh/diagnostic information — Fabric surfaces whether a model is currently operating in Direct Lake or has fallen back to Import, often visible via the model's settings or DMVs/XMLA inspection. Once confirmed, the fix is to address the actual cause in the Lakehouse pipeline: add a compaction/OPTIMIZE step after the upsert pattern to consolidate small files back into a healthy file layout, verify no unsupported data types were introduced, and re-validate the table against Direct Lake's requirements before assuming the fallback has cleared, since it generally does not revert automatically just because the table improves — it may need a model-level refresh or re-framing to re-attempt Direct Lake access.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I'd tell the BI team is: this isn't actually a Direct Lake bug, it's Direct Lake protecting itself — Fabric will silently fall back to Import mode when the underlying Delta table stops meeting its requirements, and that fallback explains both symptoms at once: it's slow now because it's doing a real import/refresh instead of reading the lake directly, and it's stale because imports only update on a schedule instead of continuously. My first move is to confirm the fallback actually happened by checking the model's diagnostic/refresh info rather than guessing, and then I go straight to the pipeline change — nine times out of ten with a timing like this, it's the new upsert pattern fragmenting the Delta table into way too many small files, which Direct Lake just won't read directly past a certain point. The real fix lives in the pipeline: add an OPTIMIZE/compaction step after the upserts so the file layout stays healthy, double check no new column introduced an unsupported type, and then re-trigger the model so it can re-attempt Direct Lake instead of assuming it'll just snap back on its own once the table's fixed.

Doesn't connect the pipeline's upsert pattern change to Delta file fragmentation as the likely trigger
Doesn't check the model's actual mode (Direct Lake vs. fallback) before proposing a fix
Assumes the model will automatically revert to Direct Lake once the table is fixed, without re-triggering
Treats slowness and staleness as two separate problems rather than one unified fallback symptom
keyPoints: Recognizes the symptom pattern as a silent Direct Lake to Import fallback
Connects the pipeline's new upsert pattern to likely Delta file fragmentation
Confirms via the model's diagnostic/mode information before prescribing a fix
Proposes a compaction/OPTIMIZE step in the pipeline as the root-cause fix
Knows the model may need explicit re-framing/refresh to re-attempt Direct Lake

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies silent Direct Lake-to-Import fallback as the mechanism
Connects pipeline upsert pattern to file fragmentation as likely trigger
Proposes correct confirmation method
Proposes correct pipeline-level fix (compaction) and re-validation step

questions.title: A Bicep Multi-Environment Deployment Fails Halfway Through Rollout
questions.prompt: A Bicep deployment pipeline promotes infrastructure changes through dev, test, and prod sequentially. The prod deployment fails partway through — a storage account resource succeeds but a dependent Fabric capacity resource times out — leaving prod in a partially-applied state while dev and test completed cleanly. Diagnose the risk this creates and design the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A partially-applied ARM/Bicep deployment leaves the resource group in a state where some resources exist with the new configuration and others are either missing, still on the old configuration, or in an intermediate provisioning state — and critically, the deployment's own history record shows 'Failed,' which can mislead whoever looks at it next into re-running the whole deployment blind, without first understanding exactly which resources did and didn't apply. The specific risk here is a dependency ordering issue: the storage account succeeded, but the Fabric capacity resource that depends on it timed out, so anything downstream of the Fabric capacity — role assignments, workspace attachments, other resources referencing its ID via dependsOn or symbolic reference — never got created or updated, meaning prod is now silently inconsistent with what the Bicep template describes, and simply re-running the deployment is the correct remedy only if the deployment is safely idempotent for every resource type involved, which is not guaranteed by default (some resource types do not tolerate a sâme-named resource provisioning request arriving while the prior one is still mid-timeout/transition). The immediate step is to check the actual deployment operations history in Azure (az deployment group show / the Deployments blade) to see the per-resource status, confirm the Fabric capacity resource's real state (did it eventually provision, or truly fail), and only then re-run the deployment — Bicep/ARM deployments are declarative and generally idempotent for a clean re-run once the timed-out resource's actual state is confirmed, but that confirmation step is the part teams skip under incident pressure. The structural fix is to add resource-level health checks or a 'what-if' deployment validation step before the real apply in the pipeline, and to make the pipeline fail fast and loud with per-resource status surfaced automatically, rather than relying on someone manually digging through the Deployments blade after the fact — and for a workload with meaningful cross-resource dependencies like Fabric capacity, consider splitting into smaller, independently-retriable deployment scopes so one slow resource's timeout doesn't gate everything downstream of it in a single deployment operation.
questions.professionalAnswer: The risk I'd flag immediately isn't 'the deployment failed,' it's that prod is now in a state the template doesn't actually describe — storage account's on the new config, but the Fabric capacity timed out, so everything that depends on that capacity never got touched. Before I just hit retry, I want to look at the actual per-resource deployment operations in Azure, not just the top-level 'Failed' status, because that tells me whether the Fabric capacity genuinely failed or is still mid-provisioning and just reported the timeout late. Bicep deployments are generally safe to re-run since they're declarative, but 'generally' isn't good enough for prod — I confirm the real state first, then re-run. The bigger fix I'd push for afterward is running `az deployment group what-if` as a gate before any prod apply so we catch this kind of thing in a dry run, and honestly, bundling a storage account and a Fabric capacity with real dependencies into one monolithic deployment is part of why one slow resource held up everything behind it — I'd rather see that split into smaller, independently retriable deployments so a timeout on one piece doesn't leave the whole environment in limbo.

Assumes the top-level 'Failed' status tells the whole story rather than checking per-resource history
Doesn't recognize downstream resources depending on the timed-out resource never got applied
Assumes all Bicep/ARM resource types are safely idempotent to retry without verification
Doesn't propose a what-if/dry-run gate or splitting deployment scope as a structural fix

Checks per-resource deployment operations/history before assuming anything about actual state

Proposes what-if validation as a pre-apply gate
Considers splitting deployment scope to limit blast radius of a single slow/dependent resource

questions.title: Eventhouse KQL Ingestion Falls Behind During a Traffic Spike
questions.prompt: A Fabric Eventhouse ingesting clickstream events via an Eventstream normally keeps ingestion lag under 10 seconds. During a flash-sale traffic spike, lag climbs to over 20 minutes, and queries against the KQL database start returning incomplete, visibly stale results even though no error is reported anywhere. Diagnose the likely bottleneck and design a fix.
questions.modelAnswer: No error being reported while lag climbs is the expected behavior of a queueing/backpressure system that is still healthy but simply under-provisioned for the current throughput — Eventhouse ingestion from an Eventstream is a pipeline with multiple stages (event ingestion into the stream, batching/staging, and the Eventhouse's own ingestion engine committing data into the KQL database), and under a traffic spike well above steady-state, any one of these stages can become the bottleneck without throwing an exception, because backpressure and queuing are the designed response to overload, not a failure. The two most common root causes are: the Eventhouse's ingestion capacity (tied to the underlying Fabric capacity's available CUs, same shared pool as every other Fabric workload on that capacity) simply doesn't have enough throughput headroom to keep up with the spike's event rate, especially if other workloads on the same capacity are also running concurrently and competing for the same CUs; or the ingestion batching policy (controlled by the database's ingestion batching settings — time, size, and count thresholds) is tuned for steady-state low-latency small batches, and under a huge spike, too many small batches get queued faster than they can be committed, creating a backlog that compounds rather than resolves on its own even after the spike ends. The investigation should check the Eventhouse's ingestion metrics (available in the Fabric Real-Time hub / Monitoring Hub) for queue depth and commit latency trends during the spike window, and cross-check whether capacity-wide CU consumption (not just this Eventhouse) spiked concurrently, which would indicate capacity contention rather than an Eventhouse-specific limit. The fix is twofold: for the immediate backlog, there may be little to do but let it drain, since killing and restarting ingestion does not recover data faster — it is a throughput-bound queue, not a stuck process; for prevention, either provision a dedicated or larger capacity for the real-time workload so it isn't competing with batch/BI workloads during spikes, and/or tune the ingestion batching policy's thresholds to match expected peak throughput rather than only steady-state averages, with alerting on ingestion lag itself (not just errors) so a growing backlog is caught in minutes, not discovered via visibly stale query results.
questions.professionalAnswer: The important thing to say out loud first is: no error doesn't mean nothing's wrong, it means the system is doing exactly what a well-built ingestion pipeline is supposed to do under overload — queue instead of fall over. So I'm not looking for a crash, I'm looking at ingestion queue depth and commit latency in the monitoring hub during the spike window, and I'm checking whether other workloads on the same Fabric capacity spiked their CU usage at the same time, because if the Eventhouse is sharing that capacity, this might not even be an Eventhouse-specific limit, it might be capacity contention. The other usual suspect is the ingestion batching policy — it's often tuned for low-latency small batches at steady state, and a huge spike can overwhelm that tuning and create a backlog that doesn't self-correct quickly just because the spike ends. For right now, there's not much to do but let the backlog drain — restarting ingestion won't make a throughput-bound queue move faster. For next time, I want either a dedicated capacity for this real-time workload so it's not fighting batch jobs for CUs during peak traffic, batching thresholds tuned for expected peak rather than average load, and critically, an alert on ingestion lag itself, because 'stale query results' is a terrible way to find out about a growing backlog twenty minutes in.

Doesn't recognize this as a queueing/backpressure scenario rather than a stuck or crashed process

Doesn't check whether other workloads on the same shared capacity are contributing to the bottleneck
Doesn't propose alerting on ingestion lag itself as a leading indicator, relying only on query freshness complaints

Checks ingestion queue depth/commit latency via monitoring, not just error logs
Considers shared-capacity CU contention as a possible root cause, not just Eventhouse-specific limits
Considers ingestion batching policy tuning as a contributing factor
Proposes dedicated capacity and/or re-tuned batching plus lag-based alerting as the durable fix

questions.title: Design a Multi-Workspace Unity Catalog Governance Model for Five Business Units
questions.prompt: You're the lead data architect for a company with five business units (Finance, Marketing, Sales, Supply Chain, HR), each running its own Databricks workspaces, migrating onto a single consolidated Unity Catalog metastore. Some data must be shared across units (a common customer dimension), some must be strictly siloed (HR compensation data), and auditors need to see exactly who accessed what. Design the catalog, schema, and access-control structure.
questions.modelAnswer: The design starts from Unity Catalog's three-level namespace (catalog.schema.table) as the primary governance boundary: I'd give each business unit its own catalog (finance, marketing, sales, supply_chain, hr), since catalog is the natural isolation boundary for access control, cost attribution, and lifecycle management in Unity Catalog, and it maps cleanly to 'who owns this data and who is accountable for it.' Within each catalog, schemas separate by sensitivity and lifecycle stage — for example hr.compensation as its own schema with the tightest grants, versus hr.directory for less sensitive org-chart data — so that a single catalog-level grant doesn't accidentally expose everything a business unit owns. For genuinely shared data like the customer dimension, I'd create a separate shared catalog (e.g., enterprise_shared) owned jointly by a data governance team rather than by any one business unit, containing conformed dimensions that need cross-unit consistency; business units read from it via GRANT SELECT at the schema or table level rather than duplicating the data, and lineage in Unity Catalog then shows exactly which downstream tables in each unit's catalog derive from that shared source. Access control follows least privilege with group-based grants, not individual-user grants — Databricks groups synced from the identity provider map to roles like finance_analysts or hr_comp_admins, and GRANT/REVOKE statements target those groups so onboarding/offboarding is a group membership change, not a per-user audit trail to maintain. For HR compensation specifically, row- and column-level security (via row filters and column masks on the table) layer on top of catalog/schema isolation for defense in depth, so even within the hr catalog, who can see raw salary figures versus aggregated-only views is enforced at the row/column level, not just the schema boundary. For audit, Unity Catalog's built-in access audit logs and lineage graph give the 'who accessed what, when, and where did it come from' answer auditors need natively, without a bespoke logging layer, as long as every workspace is actually attached to the single metastore rather than siloed metastores per unit, which is the whole point of consolidating in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I pitch this to the five business unit leads, I start with the mental model, not the implementation: catalog is 'who owns and is accountable for this,' schema is 'how sensitive/what lifecycle stage is this,' and grants are 'who, as a group, gets to touch it.' So each business unit gets its own catalog — that's their territory, and it maps directly to who I go to when there's a data quality or access question. Shared stuff, like the customer dimension everyone needs, doesn't belong inside any one unit's catalog; it goes in a jointly-owned shared catalog that a governance team owns, and units read from it instead of copying it, so when it changes, lineage shows exactly who's downstream. For HR comp data specifically, I don't rely on schema isolation alone — I'd lean on row and column-level security inside the HR catalog itself, because 'only HR can see this schema' isn't enough defense in depth for something this sensitive; I want masking even within HR for anyone who isn't specifically a comp admin. And I always push grants to groups, never individuals, because the access-review conversation six months from now needs to be 'who's in this AD group,' not 'let's manually audit forty individual grants.' The audit piece mostly falls out for free once everything's actually on one metastore — Unity Catalog's audit logs and lineage graph already answer 'who accessed what and where did it come from' without us building anything custom.
commonMistakes: Proposes separate metastores per business unit instead of one consolidated metastore with catalog-level separation
Grants access to individual users instead of identity-provider-synced groups
Relies on schema-level isolation alone for HR compensation without layering row/column-level security
Duplicates the shared customer dimension into each business unit's catalog instead of a jointly-owned shared catalog with lineage-tracked reads
Doesn't mention Unity Catalog's built-in audit logs/lineage, proposing a custom audit solution unnecessarily
keyPoints: Uses catalog as the primary per-business-unit isolation and ownership boundary
Uses schema to separate by sensitivity/lifecycle within a catalog
Proposes a jointly-owned shared catalog for conformed cross-unit dimensions, not duplication
Uses group-based GRANT/REVOKE instead of individual-user grants
Layers row/column-level security for the most sensitive data (HR comp) as defense in depth
Leverages Unity Catalog's native audit logs and lineage for auditor requirements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of catalog/schema as governance boundaries
Sound design for shared cross-unit data without duplication
Group-based least-privilege access model
Defense-in-depth for highly sensitive data (row/column security)
Addresses audit requirements via native UC capabilities

questions.title: Design a Fabric Capacity Allocation and Chargeback Model Across 30 Workspaces
questions.prompt: A managed-services company runs 30 client workspaces on Microsoft Fabric and needs to bill each client accurately for their actual compute consumption while avoiding the noisy-neighbor problems of one giant shared capacity. Design the capacity architecture and the chargeback mechanism.
questions.modelAnswer: A single shared capacity across 30 independent clients is the wrong starting point for exactly the reason the question raises: Fabric capacity consumption is pooled and smoothed across every workspace assigned to it, so one client's heavy workload degrades every other client's experience with no isolation, and attributing cost back to a specific client from a shared pool requires reconstructing per-workspace consumption after the fact rather than billing cleanly. The architecture should instead tier clients by workload profile: larger or more compute-intensive clients each get their own dedicated capacity (an F-SKU sized to their actual usage pattern, scaled via the near-instantaneous SKU change Fabric supports for predictable spend and clean isolation), while smaller, lighter clients can share a pooled capacity specifically designed for that purpose — but even in the pooled case, cost attribution should never be inferred from the pool as a whole; Fabric's capacity metrics app reports consumption broken down by workspace and by item (report, dataflow, pipeline, Spark job) within a capacity, and that per-workspace breakdown is the actual billing source of truth regardless of whether the capacity is dedicated or shared. For chargeback, I'd build a lightweight automated job that pulls the capacity metrics app's data (via its underlying semantic model or the admin APIs) on a schedule, aggregates CU-seconds consumed per workspace, and maps that to each client's invoice line item — with a clearly documented markup/margin model layered on top of raw CU cost, since clients are paying for a managed service, not just raw compute. Guardrails matter as much as the billing math: per-workspace or per-client consumption alerts so a client's own workload spike gets flagged to them specifically (rather than silently degrading someone else's pooled capacity), and a documented tier-upgrade path so a client whose usage has grown past what pooled capacity can fairly support gets moved to dedicated capacity before they become the noisy neighbor, not after a complaint.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake I'd steer this company away from immediately is one giant shared capacity for all 30 clients, because that setup makes both of the stated goals impossible at once — you can't cleanly bill for what you can't cleanly attribute, and you can't avoid noisy neighbors in a pool everyone shares. My pitch is a tiered model: bigger clients get their own dedicated capacity sized to their actual usage, which solves isolation and gives them a clean, predictable cost story; smaller clients share a pooled capacity built for that specific purpose, but even there, billing never comes from 'the pool's total cost divided somehow' — it comes from the capacity metrics app's actual per-workspace, per-item consumption breakdown, which is the real source of truth whether the capacity's shared or dedicated. I'd automate pulling that data on a schedule into whatever billing system generates client invoices, with the company's margin built in on top of raw CU cost. And I'd put alerting on per-client consumption specifically, not just capacity-wide health, so if a pooled client's usage creeps up, we catch it and talk to them about upgrading to dedicated before they start degrading somebody else's experience, instead of finding out from a complaint.
commonMistakes: Defaults to one large shared capacity for cost efficiency without addressing noisy-neighbor and attribution problems
Tries to infer per-client cost by dividing total capacity cost rather than using actual per-workspace consumption data
Doesn't use the capacity metrics app / admin APIs as the billing source of truth
Proposes dedicated capacity for every client regardless of usage size, overspending on light clients
No per-client consumption alerting, so noisy-neighbor issues are discovered via complaints rather than proactively
keyPoints: Tiers clients into dedicated vs. pooled capacity based on actual workload profile
Uses capacity metrics app per-workspace/per-item data as the billing source of truth, not pool-wide estimates
Automates chargeback aggregation from real consumption data into client invoicing
Builds in margin/markup over raw CU cost explicitly
Adds per-client consumption alerting and a documented tier-upgrade path to prevent noisy-neighbor issues proactively

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rejects single shared capacity for this use case with sound reasoning
Proposes a sound tiered dedicated/pooled architecture
Uses accurate per-workspace consumption data as the chargeback basis
Proposes proactive monitoring/upgrade path to prevent noisy-neighbor issues

questions.title: Design a Multi-Datacenter Kafka Replication Architecture With Schema Governance
questions.prompt: A company operates Kafka clusters in three datacenters (US-East, US-West, EU) for regulatory data-residency and latency reasons, but needs a consistent view of certain global topics (like a product catalog) across all three, plus a single governed schema evolution process that doesn't let any one region break the others. Design the replication topology and schema governance model, and justify active/active versus active/passive for the topics involved.
questions.modelAnswer: The topology decision should be made per-topic-class, not globally, because 'active/active vs active/passive' is really a question about who legitimately produces to a topic. For genuinely global, single-source-of-truth data like a product catalog, I'd use active/passive replication (via a tool like MirrorMaker 2 or a managed cross-region replication service): one region is authoritative and produces to the canonical topic, and the other two regions consume a replicated, read-only copy — this avoids the conflict-resolution problem entirely, since there is never a case where the same key is written independently in two regions and needs reconciling. For topics where each region genuinely needs to produce its own regional data that must also be visible globally (e.g., regional order events that roll up into a global reporting topic), active/active replication is appropriate, but only with a deliberate partitioning/keying strategy that guarantees no two regions ever own the same partition or key space, so active/active never actually means 'conflicting concurrent writes to the same record' — it means 'independent writes to disjoint key spaces that get aggregated,' which sidesteps the hard conflict-resolution problem that true multi-master systems face. Regulatory data residency constrains this further: PII or regulated data that must stay in-region per compliance never gets replicated at all; only the global reference/catalog-type topics cross regional boundaries. For schema governance, a single global schema registry cluster (replicated across regions, or a managed service with multi-region support) should be the system of record for every topic's schema, with compatibility mode set to FULL for globally-replicated topics specifically, since both the authoritative region's producers and every consuming region's consumers must remain mutually compatible — a region-local, weaker compatibility mode on a globally-replicated topic is exactly how one region's local schema change silently breaks consumers in another region. Schema changes to any globally-replicated topic should go through a change-management process requiring sign-off from a cross-region data governance owner, not just the originating region's team, precisely because a change that looks safe locally can break consumers thousands of miles away who have no visibility into that team's release process.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to refuse to answer 'active/active or active/passive' as one global decision, because it's really a per-topic question about who's actually authoritative. For something like the product catalog, there's exactly one source of truth, so active/passive is the obvious and simplest choice — one region produces, the other two get a replicated read-only copy via MirrorMaker 2 or a managed replication service, and there's no conflict resolution to design because there's never a conflicting write. Where I would consider active/active is for genuinely regional data that rolls up globally, like per-region order events, but only if I can guarantee each region owns a disjoint key space — active/active for me never means 'two regions might write the same key,' because that's a conflict-resolution problem I don't want to own if I can design around it. Data residency adds a hard constraint underneath all of this: anything regulated stays in-region, full stop, only the genuinely global reference data crosses borders. On schema governance, I want one registry as the system of record across all three regions, and for any topic that's globally replicated, I'm setting FULL compatibility, not backward-only, because a globally-replicated topic has producers and consumers in different regions who absolutely need mutual compatibility in both directions — and any schema change to one of those topics needs a sign-off from someone who can see the whole picture, not just the originating region's own release process.
commonMistakes: Picks one topology (active/active or active/passive) globally instead of deciding per topic class based on authoritative ownership
Proposes active/active without a disjoint key-space/partitioning strategy, reintroducing the conflict-resolution problem
Doesn't account for data-residency constraints preventing regulated data from replicating across regions at all
Proposes region-local schema registries instead of a single governed registry as system of record
Uses backward-only compatibility for globally-replicated topics instead of FULL, missing the bidirectional need
keyPoints: Decides topology per topic class based on authoritative ownership, not as one global choice
Uses active/passive for single-source-of-truth global data (e.g. product catalog)
If using active/active, requires a disjoint key-space strategy to avoid real conflict resolution
Respects data-residency constraints by excluding regulated data from cross-region replication
Uses a single governed schema registry with FULL compatibility for globally-replicated topics
Requires cross-region governance sign-off for schema changes to global topics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons topology choice per topic class, not globally
Sound active/passive vs active/active justification with conflict-avoidance reasoning
Correctly incorporates data-residency constraints
Sound schema governance model (single registry, FULL compatibility, cross-region sign-off)

questions.title: Design a Terraform Module Registry and Drift Detection Strategy for a 50-Person Platform Team
questions.prompt: A platform team of 50 engineers across multiple squads provisions Databricks, Fabric, and Kafka infrastructure via Terraform, but modules are currently copy-pasted between repos, drift between what's in state and what's actually deployed is discovered only when something breaks, and promoting a change from dev to prod is manual and inconsistent. Design the module registry, drift detection, and promotion strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: The copy-paste problem is solved by a private module registry (Terraform Cloud's registry, an internal Git-based registry, or an artifact-repository-backed one) where each infrastructure primitive — a Fabric capacity, a Databricks workspace with its standard cluster policies, a Kafka cluster with standard topic conventions — is published as a versioned module with semantic versioning, so squads consume a specific pinned version (source = "app.terraform.io/org/databricks-workspace/azurerm", version = "~> 2.1") instead of copying raw HCL, and a breaking change to the module requires an explicit major version bump that consuming squads opt into on their own schedule rather than inheriting silently. Drift detection needs to run continuously and proactively, not be discovered via an incident: a scheduled job (nightly, via CI) running terraform plan (or plan -refresh-only) against every environment's state, with any detected drift posted automatically to a shared channel and logged, turns 'we found out prod didn't match state when it broke' into 'we got an alert at 2am that something changed outside Terraform.' For promotion, environments should be structured as a strict pipeline — dev, test, prod as separate state files/workspaces per environment, never a single state file spanning environments — and a change flows through a required sequence: PR against the module or the environment config triggers a plan in dev, which is applied automatically on merge; the same commit then requires an explicit promotion gate (manual approval or automated test-suite pass) before the identical plan output is applied to test, and again before prod, so the exact same reviewed artifact — not a re-authored one — moves through each stage. Policy-as-code (Sentinel, OPA, or Terraform's native validation blocks) should gate every plan in CI before apply, enforcing organization rules like 'every Fabric capacity must have cost tags' or 'every Kafka cluster module version must be >= 2.0' automatically, rather than relying on manual PR review to catch convention violations across 50 engineers. The registry, drift detection, and promotion pipeline together turn infrastructure changes from an artisanal, inconsistent process into a governed, observable one, which is the actual problem at this team size — copy-paste and manual promotion do not scale past a handful of engineers without producing exactly the drift and inconsistency described.
questions.professionalAnswer: At 50 engineers, the copy-paste problem is the thing I'd fix first, because it's the root of basically everything else — if every squad has their own slightly-different copy of a Databricks workspace module, you don't have one thing to version, test, or gate, you have fifty things quietly drifting apart. So step one is a private module registry with real semantic versioning, so squads pin a version and a breaking change requires an explicit, visible major bump they choose to adopt, not something that silently lands on their next apply. For drift, I don't want to find out prod doesn't match state because something broke — I want a nightly plan-only job against every environment's state that posts to a channel the moment it sees anything unexpected, so drift is a Tuesday-morning Slack message, not a Friday-night incident. For promotion, I'm structuring dev/test/prod as genuinely separate state, and the thing that moves between them is the exact same reviewed plan output, not a re-run that might produce something slightly different — merge to dev auto-applies, then there's an explicit gate before the identical change goes to test, then another before prod. And I'd put policy-as-code in front of every single plan in CI, because at this scale I can't rely on fifty engineers all remembering the same tagging and versioning conventions in every PR review — the automation needs to enforce it, not the reviewer's memory.
commonMistakes: Proposes only 'better documentation' or conventions instead of an actual versioned module registry
Doesn't propose scheduled, automated drift detection, relying on incident discovery
Uses a single state file/workspace spanning multiple environments instead of separate state per environment
Promotion pipeline re-runs/re-authors the plan per environment instead of promoting the exact same reviewed artifact
Relies on manual PR review alone for convention enforcement instead of policy-as-code gates in CI
keyPoints: Proposes a versioned private module registry to eliminate copy-paste modules
Proposes scheduled, automated drift detection (plan-only) with proactive alerting
Uses separate state per environment with a strict, gated promotion sequence
Promotes the same reviewed plan artifact through environments rather than re-running independently
Adds policy-as-code gates in CI to enforce org conventions automatically at scale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sound versioned module registry solving the copy-paste problem
Proposes proactive, automated drift detection
Sound environment separation and gated promotion pipeline design
Proposes policy-as-code enforcement appropriate to team scale

questions.title: Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines vs. Fabric-Native Pipelines: Making the Call
questions.prompt: Your organization already has both a Databricks workspace and a Fabric tenant in production. A new workload needs to ingest and transform semi-structured IoT sensor data (roughly 50GB/day, with moderate but real data-quality requirements) into a form both data scientists and BI analysts can use. Decide between building it as a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline or a Fabric-native pipeline (Dataflow Gen2 + Data Factory-style pipeline), and justify the tradeoffs explicitly.
questions.modelAnswer: This decision should hinge on three real differentiators rather than brand preference: declarative data-quality enforcement, who the primary downstream consumers are, and which platform already owns the compute/governance context this workload needs to integrate with. Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines have first-class, declarative data-quality expectations (warn/drop/fail) wired directly into the pipeline definition, version-controlled lineage through Unity Catalog, and native support for both batch and continuous/streaming triggering modes from the same pipeline definition — given the stated 'moderate but real data-quality requirements,' that declarative expectations model is a meaningful advantage over hand-rolling data-quality checks as separate pipeline steps, which is closer to what a Fabric-native Dataflow Gen2 + pipeline combination would require. On the consumption side, if data scientists are a primary audience, Databricks' notebook-native Python/SQL environment, MLflow integration, and direct Delta table access without any semantic-model intermediary make Lakeflow materially better-suited; if BI analysts via Power BI with Direct Lake performance are the primary and growing audience, Fabric-native pipelines keep the data in OneLake with a shorter path to a Direct Lake semantic model, avoiding an extra hop (Databricks Delta tables surfaced into Fabric via shortcuts) that Lakeflow would otherwise require for that audience. Given the question states both audiences exist, the practical answer is: build the ingestion and quality-enforcement stage in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, landing clean, validated, governed Delta tables in Unity Catalog — then expose those tables into Fabric via a OneLake shortcut (which does not duplicate the data) for Direct Lake-mode BI consumption, giving data scientists native Databricks access and BI analysts Direct Lake performance from the same underlying Delta tables without choosing one platform exclusively. This hybrid is justified specifically because the data-quality requirements favor Lakeflow's declarative expectations as the ingestion/cleaning layer, while OneLake shortcuts make 'pick one platform for everything downstream' an unnecessary and worse tradeoff than using each platform for what it does best.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't frame this as 'Databricks or Fabric' — I'd frame it as 'where does data quality get enforced, and where does each audience actually need to touch the data.' Given there's a real data-quality requirement here, Lakeflow's declarative expectations are a genuine edge — warn/drop/fail wired right into the pipeline definition beats hand-building quality checks as separate steps in a Fabric pipeline. So my instinct is: do the ingestion and cleaning in Lakeflow, land it as governed Delta tables in Unity Catalog. But I'm not going to make data scientists and BI analysts fight over which platform 'wins,' because I don't have to — I'd shortcut those Delta tables into OneLake, which doesn't copy any data, and that gets BI analysts Direct Lake performance in Power BI while data scientists keep working natively in Databricks against the same underlying tables. The real tradeoff I'm making explicit to the team is: we're not choosing one platform for this workload, we're using Lakeflow specifically because of the data-quality requirement, and OneLake shortcuts specifically so that decision doesn't force a worse experience on the BI side.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a binary platform choice rather than evaluating specific differentiators (data quality, audience, integration)
Doesn't mention Lakeflow's declarative expectations as the specific advantage relevant to the stated data-quality requirement
Picks Fabric-native for BI convenience without considering OneLake shortcuts as a way to avoid an exclusive choice
Proposes duplicating data between platforms instead of using a shortcut/zero-copy approach
Ignores that both audiences (data scientists and BI analysts) are explicitly named as needing to use this data
keyPoints: Evaluates the decision on data-quality enforcement, audience, and platform-integration fit, not brand preference
Identifies Lakeflow's declarative expectations as the specific advantage for real data-quality requirements
Identifies Databricks as the better native fit for data-scientist consumption
Identifies Fabric/Direct Lake as the better native fit for BI-analyst consumption
Proposes a hybrid using OneLake shortcuts to avoid an unnecessary exclusive platform choice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Evaluates on concrete differentiators rather than platform preference
Correctly ties data-quality requirement to Lakeflow's declarative expectations advantage
Correctly reasons about audience fit for each platform
Proposes a sound hybrid using OneLake shortcuts rather than an exclusive choice

questions.title: Design Exactly-Once Ingestion From Kafka Into a Delta Lakehouse at Scale
questions.prompt: Design an ingestion pipeline that reads payment-event records from a high-throughput Kafka topic (roughly 20,000 events/sec at peak) into a Delta Lake table, with a hard requirement that no payment event is ever duplicated or lost in the target table, even across consumer crashes, cluster restarts, and Kafka broker failovers.
questions.modelAnswer: Exactly-once end-to-end from Kafka into Delta requires chaining two separate exactly-once mechanisms correctly, because neither Kafka's exactly-once producer guarantee nor Delta's transactional guarantees alone span the whole pipeline. On the read side, I'd use Databricks Structured Streaming (or an equivalent Lakeflow streaming flow) reading from Kafka with checkpointing enabled against a durable checkpoint location (cloud storage, not local disk) — the checkpoint records exactly which Kafka offsets have been durably committed into Delta, and on restart after any crash, Structured Streaming resumes from the last committed checkpoint offset rather than the consumer group's own committed offset, which is what gives it crash-safe, exactly-once-from-the-source-topic semantics rather than relying on Kafka consumer group offset commits (which can drift out of sync with what was actually durably written downstream). On the write side, Delta Lake's ACID transaction log means each micro-batch write either fully commits or doesn't happen at all, so a crash mid-write never leaves a half-written batch visible to readers — combined with Structured Streaming's checkpoint-offset coordination, a batch is either fully committed to Delta with its offset range marked done, or the whole batch (data and offset progress) is retried from scratch, which is what prevents both duplicates and gaps across the Kafka-to-Delta boundary specifically. For genuine defense in depth against any remaining edge case (e.g., a schema that allows a payment event's natural key to be known), I'd add an idempotent merge pattern as a second layer: write micro-batches to a staging table, then MERGE INTO the target table using the payment event's unique transaction ID as the match key, so even in some theoretical edge case where the same offset range got reprocessed, the merge's upsert-on-key semantics make reprocessing a no-op rather than a duplicate row. At 20,000 events/sec, partition the Kafka topic and the Structured Streaming job's parallelism to match (sufficient Kafka partitions and Spark task parallelism to avoid becoming consumer-lag-bound), and size the Delta table's file layout (via OPTIMIZE/auto-compaction) to avoid the small-file problem that high-frequency micro-batch commits would otherwise create over time.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about 'exactly-once from Kafka into Delta' is that it's actually two separate guarantees that need to be chained correctly, not one single setting I flip on. On the read side, I want Structured Streaming's checkpointing, pointed at durable cloud storage, because that's what gives me 'resume exactly where I left off' after a crash — critically, resuming from the checkpoint's committed offset, not from Kafka's own consumer group offset, which can get out of sync with what actually landed in Delta. On the write side, Delta's transaction log means a micro-batch either fully commits or it doesn't happen at all, so there's no such thing as a half-written batch becoming visible — and because Structured Streaming ties offset progress to that same transactional commit, a crash mid-batch means the whole batch retries, not a duplicate-or-gap situation. For something as sensitive as payment events, though, I don't stop there — I'd add a MERGE INTO using the payment's unique transaction ID as the key, so even in some edge case I haven't thought of, reprocessing the same event becomes a no-op upsert instead of a duplicate row. That's the belt-and-suspenders answer: checkpoint-coordinated streaming for the primary exactly-once guarantee, idempotent merge on a real business key as the safety net. And at this volume, I'm also paying attention to Kafka partition count and Spark parallelism matching up, plus compaction on the Delta side, because high-frequency micro-batches will absolutely create a small-file problem if nobody's watching the file layout.
commonMistakes: Relies on Kafka consumer group offset commits alone instead of Structured Streaming's checkpoint-based offset tracking
Assumes Delta's transactional guarantee alone is sufficient without addressing read-side offset/crash coordination
Doesn't propose an idempotent merge/upsert-by-business-key as defense in depth for a payment-sensitive use case
Ignores the small-file problem that high-frequency micro-batch commits create without compaction
Doesn't address partition/parallelism sizing for the stated 20,000 events/sec throughput
keyPoints: Uses Structured Streaming checkpointing against durable storage for crash-safe offset tracking
Explains why checkpoint-coordinated offsets beat relying on Kafka consumer group commits alone
Uses Delta's ACID transaction log to guarantee all-or-nothing micro-batch commits
Adds idempotent MERGE INTO on a business key as defense-in-depth for payment-sensitive data
Addresses partition/parallelism sizing and file-layout/compaction for the stated throughput

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs checkpoint-based exactly-once read coordination
Correctly explains Delta's transactional write guarantee role
Proposes idempotent merge as defense-in-depth for payment data
Addresses scale considerations (partitioning, parallelism, compaction)

questions.title: Design a Hybrid Lambda/Kappa Architecture Spanning Databricks, Kafka, and Fabric
questions.prompt: A retail analytics platform needs both real-time inventory alerts (sub-minute latency) and accurate, fully-reconciled daily sales reporting (which can tolerate hours of latency but must be exactly correct, including late-arriving and corrected records). Design an architecture spanning Kafka, Databricks, and Fabric that serves both needs without duplicating business logic across two incompatible codebases.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a textbook case for a hybrid lambda-leaning-kappa architecture rather than a pure lambda (two separate codebases, batch and streaming, that inevitably drift) or a pure kappa (reprocess everything through the stream, which struggles with 'must be exactly correct including corrections' requirements that need true reconciliation against a complete historical record). The design: Kafka is the single ingestion point for all sales/inventory events, with every event — including late-arriving and corrected records — flowing through one topic as the system of record. From there, a streaming Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline (or Structured Streaming job) consumes the topic continuously for the sub-minute inventory-alert path, applying business logic (stock threshold checks, alerting) directly on the stream and writing to a low-latency serving table (or directly triggering an alert) — this path intentionally does not wait for late data, since the alerting use case explicitly tolerates some imprecision in exchange for speed. The same business logic for core transformations (not duplicated separately) is expressed once, in a shared Lakeflow pipeline definition that also runs in batch/triggered mode on a schedule (e.g., every few hours or nightly) against the full historical Delta table, reprocessing with watermarking and late-arrival handling to produce the fully-reconciled daily sales figures — because Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines can express the same declarative transformation logic for both continuous and triggered/batch execution from one definition, the 'two codebases drifting' problem that classic lambda architectures suffer from is avoided; it's the same pipeline logic run at two different cadences against two different completeness guarantees, not two hand-maintained implementations. The reconciled daily output lands in a governed Delta table in Unity Catalog, then surfaces into Fabric via a OneLake shortcut for BI reporting with Direct Lake performance, while the fast inventory-alert path can either stay purely in the streaming layer (Kafka Streams/ksqlDB-style) or also be exposed through Fabric's real-time Eventstream/Eventhouse path if BI-adjacent dashboards also need the fast-moving view. The key architectural discipline is: one source of truth (the Kafka topic), one transformation logic definition (the Lakeflow pipeline, run at two cadences), and two serving paths tuned for their actual latency/correctness tradeoff, rather than two independently-maintained pipelines that will inevitably produce different numbers for the same underlying events.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trap I'd steer this team away from is building two separate pipelines — one 'fast and approximate,' one 'slow and correct' — because that's classic lambda architecture, and the two will drift apart in subtle ways within six months no matter how disciplined the team is. My actual design: Kafka is the one system of record for every event, including corrections and late arrivals. The core transformation logic gets written once, as a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline definition, and that same definition runs two ways — continuously, against the live stream, for the sub-minute inventory alerts, where I'm explicitly trading completeness for speed because that's what the use case needs; and on a scheduled batch cadence against the full historical Delta table, with proper watermarking for late/corrected records, for the fully-reconciled daily sales numbers. Same logic, two cadences, two different completeness guarantees — not two codebases somebody has to keep in sync by hand. The reconciled output lands in Unity Catalog and gets shortcut into Fabric for BI, Direct Lake and all, with no data duplication. The discipline I'd defend hardest in design review is: one source of truth, one transformation definition, two serving paths — the moment someone proposes a second independent pipeline for 'just the fast path,' that's where lambda architectures start quietly lying to different audiences.
commonMistakes: Builds two independently-maintained pipelines (classic lambda) that will drift and produce inconsistent numbers
Doesn't recognize Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines can express one transformation definition run at both continuous and batch cadence
Proposes a pure kappa/stream-only approach without addressing the explicit need for true reconciliation of late/corrected records
Doesn't identify Kafka as the single system-of-record ingestion point for all events including corrections
Duplicates data between Databricks and Fabric instead of using a OneLake shortcut
keyPoints: Uses Kafka as the single system-of-record ingestion point for all events, including late/corrected ones
Expresses core transformation logic once via a Lakeflow pipeline definition, run at two cadences

questions.title: Design a DR/Failover Strategy Spanning Databricks, Fabric, and Kafka
questions.prompt: Design a disaster recovery strategy for a production data platform where Kafka is the ingestion backbone, Databricks runs the core transformation/ML workloads, and Fabric serves the BI layer — such that a regional Azure outage can be survived with a defined, defensible RTO/RPO, and no single component's recovery plan was designed in isolation from the others.
questions.modelAnswer: The most common DR mistake at this scope is designing each component's recovery plan independently, which produces three technically-correct-in-isolation plans that don't actually compose into a working recovery, because the real dependency graph runs through all three: Fabric's BI layer depends on Databricks' Delta tables (or OneLake shortcuts to them) being available and current, and Databricks' transformations depend on Kafka's events having actually arrived and been processed up to some known point. So the design has to start from the dependency chain, not each platform's individual failover feature. For Kafka, I'd run a cross-region cluster setup (via MirrorMaker 2 or a managed multi-region offering) with the secondary region continuously replicating from the primary, so that on a regional outage, producers and consumers can fail over to the secondary region's replicated topics with a known replication lag defining the RPO for the ingestion layer specifically — that lag number is the hard floor for every downstream RPO claim, since nothing downstream can recover data that never reached Kafka's secondary region. For Databricks, Unity Catalog and Delta tables backed by geo-redundant cloud storage (GRS/RA-GRS) give the underlying data durability across regions, but the workspace and its job definitions, cluster policies, and Lakeflow pipeline definitions also need to exist in a secondary-region workspace, provisioned via the same Terraform/Bicep IaC used for the primary — DR for compute infrastructure should never be a manual, undocumented rebuild under pressure; it's the same IaC applied to a secondary region's resource group, validated with periodic actual failover drills, not just a plan on paper. For Fabric, since capacity is region-scoped, a secondary capacity in the DR region needs to exist (or be provisionable quickly) with its own OneLake and semantic models pointed at the Databricks DR region's Delta tables, and the actual cutover for BI consumers (DNS/connection string changes, or Fabric's own regional routing if available) needs to be included in the same failover runbook as the Kafka and Databricks steps, not a separate BI-team-only plan. The RTO/RPO numbers that get presented to the business must be the composite of the slowest, highest-lag component in this chain — if Kafka's cross-region replication lag is 5 minutes but Databricks' DR workspace takes 45 minutes to actually fail over to, the platform's real RTO is 45+ minutes regardless of how fast Kafka recovers, and that composite number, not each component's individual best case, is the number that should go in the DR plan.
questions.professionalAnswer: The failure mode I'd actively design against here is three separate teams each bringing me a technically-sound DR plan for their own piece — Kafka team's plan, Databricks team's plan, Fabric team's plan — that don't actually compose, because BI depends on Databricks depends on Kafka, and nobody's plan accounts for that chain. So I start by mapping the dependency, not the components: Fabric needs current Databricks output, Databricks needs Kafka events that actually arrived. For Kafka, cross-region replication with MirrorMaker 2 or a managed equivalent gives me a concrete replication-lag number, and that number is the real floor on everything downstream's RPO — nothing recovers data Kafka's secondary region never got. For Databricks, the data durability mostly comes from geo-redundant storage under Unity Catalog, but the workspace itself — jobs, cluster policies, pipeline definitions — needs to exist in the DR region too, and I want that provisioned by the same Terraform we use for primary, not someone's memory of how the workspace was configured eighteen months ago. Fabric needs its own DR-region capacity with OneLake and semantic models already pointed at wherever Databricks' DR region lands. And the number I actually bring to leadership isn't any one team's best-case RTO — it's the composite of the slowest link in that whole chain, because that's the real number, and I want everyone's failover runbook to be one document, tested with an actual drill, not three documents that have never been run together.
commonMistakes: Designs each platform's DR plan in isolation without mapping the actual cross-platform dependency chain
Reports each component's best-case RTO/RPO individually instead of the composite across the dependency chain
Treats Delta/storage durability (GRS) as sufficient DR without also covering workspace/job/pipeline-definition recovery via IaC
Doesn't account for Fabric capacity being region-scoped, requiring its own DR-region provisioning
No mention of periodic actual failover drills, relying on an untested paper plan
keyPoints: Maps the real cross-platform dependency chain (Fabric depends on Databricks depends on Kafka) before designing per-component plans
Uses cross-region Kafka replication with a defined replication lag as the ingestion-layer RPO floor
Covers both data durability (GRS) and workspace/pipeline-definition recovery (via IaC) for Databricks
Addresses Fabric's region-scoped capacity requiring its own DR provisioning
Reports the composite, slowest-link RTO/RPO rather than each component's individual best case
Recommends periodic actual failover drills, not just a paper plan

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly maps cross-platform dependency chain driving the design
Sound Kafka cross-region replication and RPO reasoning
Sound Databricks DR design covering both data and workspace/IaC recovery
Sound Fabric DR-region capacity design
Correctly reasons about composite RTO/RPO and need for drills
